utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, Mr. Zecevic and I are here this morning on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic pursuant to Rule 98 bis requesting that you acquit Mr. Milutinovic on all counts in the indictment. Rule 98 bis provides, and I quote: "At the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction." What is the degree of proof necessary under Rule 98 bis? We refer the Chamber to two precedents, two oral decisions under Rule 98 bis, the first is from the Mrksic case IT-98-13/1-T, transcript 11311 to 11313. The second decision is from the Martic case, that's case IT-95-11-T, the transcript reference is 5960 to 5961. I'll quote from the Mrksic case at 11311. "The standard to be applied in respect of each count is whether on the evidence as it stands and taken at its highest for the Prosecution, it would be properly open to a Trial Chamber to be persuaded beyond reasonable doubt to convict the accused. "It follows that a decision that there is evidence capable of sustaining a conviction on a particular count is in no sense an indication of the view of this Chamber as to the ultimate guilt or innocence of the accused on that count. This is so because at this stage of the case the Chamber is not to evaluate the respective credit of witnesses or the strengths and weaknesses of contradictory or different evidence. The Chamber is required at this stage to assume that the Prosecution's evidence is, and I quote, 'entitled to credence unless incapable of belief.' "In essence, a Rule 98 bis motion will succeed if there is no evidence supporting a particular count, or if the only relevant evidence is so incapable of belief that it could not properly sustain a conviction, even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution." The Mrksic Chamber goes on to rely on the Jelisic Appeals Chamber decision, the Strugar Trial Chamber decision, and the Milosevic Trial Chamber decision. The Martic Trial Chamber adopted the language from Mrksic and at 11312 of the Mrksic transcript the Chamber said that: "This may be established even though the evidence is not necessarily sufficient in respect of some other allegations or particulars set out in the indictment in respect of that count or in respect of one or some forms of criminal responsibility relied on by the Prosecution. The Prosecution need only ultimately succeed in proving one form or one of the forms of criminal responsibility it relies on for there to be a conviction on a count. We say, therefore, that a 98 bis motion will succeed if there's no evidence supporting a particular count or if the only relevant evidence is so incapable of belief that it could not properly sustain a conviction even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution. The indictment against Mr. Milutinovic contains five counts: Count 1 is deportation; Count 2 is forcible transfer; Counts 3 and 4 are murder; Count 5 is persecutions. Each of the five counts incorporates paragraphs from the indictment in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. Paragraphs 1 and 8 detail the -- Mr. Milutinovic's background, his position; paragraphs 16 to 23 his individual responsibility; 24 to 34 are the overview of the JCE; and 35 to 40 are specific allegations against Mr. Milutinovic. Mr. Milutinovic is charged under Article 7(1) for planning, instigating, ordering, committing as a co-perpetrator in a JCE, or otherwise aiding and abetting. He's also charged under 7(3) as having superior authority for the alleged crimes set out in Counts 1 to 5. In our submission, there is no evidence of planning, instigating, ordering, committing, or aiding and abetting in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. There is no evidence of any superior authority in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. As a matter of fact and law, we say he's not guilty and you should acquit him at this stage. I propose to review the evidence in this case, but before doing that I remind the Court that in our pre-trial brief we stipulated to certain facts. That was our 65 ter (F) filing on the 6th of June 2006 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one matter before you proceed. Is there any extent to which your submission is a joint submission for all the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the law may be presented differently by the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I don't believe so, not the law, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The facts to which we have stipulated, pre-trial, is that Mr. Milutinovic served at the SFRY Ambassador to Greece from the 15th of June, 1989, until the 27th of April, 1992, and thereafter as the FRY Ambassador to Greece until the 15th of August, 1995. He was appointed Minister of Foreign Affairs of the FRY on the 15th of June, 1995. Mr. Milutinovic was elected president of the Republic of Serbia and served in that function from 21 December 1997 until 29 December 2002. And as the president of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic was a member of the Supreme Defence Council of the FRY. So we have agreed that Mr. Milutinovic was the president of the Republic of Serbia and that he was a member of the Supreme Defence Council. Those are the two facts that are relevant to this case in particular. I'll be making detailed submissions about the Supreme Defence Council. At this point I'll say that evidence in this case is that there's no evidence that the Supreme Defence Council met or functioned after the 23rd of March, 1999. I'll review the powers and authorities of the Supreme Defence Council by reference to the constitutions of the FRY and Serbia, the relevant legislation, minutes of meetings of the Supreme Defence Council, and the testimony of OTP witnesses. In addition, the Prosecution alleges that Mr. Milutinovic was a member of a body called the Supreme Command; there's no evidence of that. These allegations are set out in paragraphs 36 and 37 of the indictment. There's no evidence that Mr. Milutinovic was a member of such a body and there's no evidence that such a body existed. I turn first to submissions in response to the allegations contained in the indictment concerning Mr. Milutinovic as the president of Serbia. Paragraph 8(i) of the indictment says that: "Mr. Milutinovic was the head of state. He represented Serbia and conducted its relations with foreign states and international organisations." Let's look at the evidence in this case in relation to this paragraph. I prefer the Chamber first to Exhibit P855, that's the constitution of the Republic of Serbia that came into effect on the 28th of September, 1990. Article 1 says that the Republic of Serbia is a state. Article 9(2) says that: "The Republic of Serbia is represented and its state unity symbolised by the President of the republic." Now, it's correct that the Republic of Serbia is a state. For our purposes, it's always been a state, a constituent element of a federal state. It was first a constituent republic in the SFRY, and on the 27th of April, 1992, Serbia was a constituent element of the new state of the FRY. In other words, Serbia has never had an international personality; it's never been a sovereign state. We say the president of Serbia did not conduct its relations with foreign states and international organisations. For more clarity, we ask the Chamber to look at P1623, which is the constitution of the FRY -- SFRY, 1974. Article 281, subparagraph 7, says that: "The federal -- the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ensured foreign policy on behalf of that federal state." Not the Republic of Serbia when Serbia was a constituent republic of that federal state. We refer you to P856 which is the constitution of the FRY, which is dated 27 April 1992. There again a review of that constitution, that federal constitution, shows you that the FRY organs are competent in the area of international relations. I refer you to Article 77, subparagraph 6. Article 96, subparagraph 1 says: "The President of FRY represents the FRY at home and abroad." Article 99, subparagraph 1 of the constitution says: "The federal government establishes and conducts foreign and domestic policies." One might ask then why and where did the Prosecution, and on what did it base paragraph 8(i) of its indictment. Well, that requires a review and an understanding of the relationship between the constitution of the FRY and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. Because if one turns to the constitution of Serbia, P855, at Article 83, subparagraph 4, you see this, it says that: "The President of the Republic shall conduct affairs in the sphere of relations between the Republic of Serbia and other states and international organisations in accordance with the law." Well, this particular article of the Serbian constitution has no implementing legislation; it was never given any effect in law. So there seems to be an apparent conflict between the Serbian constitution and the FRY constitution, but that's regulated by law. That's regulated by Article 135 of the Serbian constitution, P855. There is a paramountcy clause that says in the case of conflict the federal jurisdiction has primacy over the constituent republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you arguing that a constitution such as the constitution of Serbia requires some other form of legislation before a particular provision in it takes effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, in relation to Article 83 it says it would be regulated in accordance with law, so that was the specific reference there to that particular section of the Serbian constitution. So at the time that there was -- Serbia was part of the SFRY, it was regulated by a clause which recognised the paramountcy of the federal constitution. The same is true if you look at the federal constitution of the FRY, P856. I refer you -- I ask you to look at Article 7; 16; 78(2), (3), and (4); 92, subparagraph 2; 115; and 130. All those provisions of the federal constitution of the FRY show that the -- in the case of conflict between the two constitutions, the federal constitution is paramount. We say that on a proper construction and interpretation, one must understand that the Serbian constitution of 1990 has to be understood in the political events that were unfolding in the former Yugoslavia at the time. In 1990, the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia was taking place and there are provisions in the Serbian constitution that provide for two possibilities. One is the Republic of Serbia remaining in a federal state or the Republic of Serbia becoming an independent state, and therefore there are provisions that on the face of it might lead one to conclude that there are powers given to organs and entities in Serbia which are consistent with an independent sovereign state. But I repeat that there are clauses on paramountcy that explain that if Serbia were to remain in a federal unit, which it always did, the SFRY and the FRY, then the federal bodies and organs and personalities are paramount. So in relation to paragraph 8, subparagraph i, of the indictment, there's no evidence that Mr. Milutinovic was a head of state. He never conducted Serbian relations with foreign states, and he never exercised such powers either. I turn then to paragraph 8, subparagraph iii, of the indictment, which says that: "Mr. Milutinovic, in conjunction with the Republic of Serbia Assembly, had the authority to request reports both from the Government of Serbia concerning matters under its jurisdiction and from the MUP, concerning its activities and the security situation in Serbia." Here the constitution of Serbia, P855, is quite specific. I address your attention to Article 83, subparagraph 12, which confers powers on the president and here there are powers that are confined by the constitution. Article 83(12) says that: "The President of the Republic shall conduct affairs in accordance with the constitution." His powers are laid down by the constitution, not by statute. Statute will define the details of a power vested in a constitution, but statute may not create a power for the President of the Republic of Serbia. There is one power given to the president of the Republic of Serbia under the constitution in relation to the government and that's in Article 85. Article 85 of the Serbian constitution says: "The President of the Republic may request from the government to state its viewpoints concerning some questions following within its jurisdiction." Now, I emphasise that the wording says: "The President may request a viewpoint from the government," he may not order. Nowhere in the legislation of the constitution does the president of the republic have the power or influence or the ability to influence the government to amend or abandon a viewpoint. The president has no ability to ask for any further information once given by the government. Nowhere in the legislative framework of the country does the president of Serbia have the ability or the institution to verify the completeness or veracity of information. This power is regulated by law, and that is P1862, the Law on Government. Article 19 provides the means for the president to exercise the power vested by Article 85 of the Serbian constitution. It says: "The government acting upon a request from the President of the Republic and within a time-limit set by the President of the Republic, which may not be shorter than 48 hours, adopts a position concerning an issue falling under its sphere of competence and informs the President of the Republic accordingly." Now, the Law on Government sets out many things. It says that the government, and not the president, has the power and responsibility over matters of public administration. The president has no constitutional or statutory authority over public administration or public authorities and they owe no duty to the president of the republic. The government under this law, the Law on Government, appoints and dismisses ministers and other administrative individuals and bodies. It's responsible for financing, it controls and supervises ministries, and it establishes principles for the internal organisation of ministries and other administrative bodies. And what of the relationship between the president of Serbia and the Ministry of the Interior? Again, it's a statutory relationship, not constitutional. P1737 is the Law on Internal Affairs; it sets out the framework. Article 1, subparagraph 2, says: "The minister -- the Ministry of the Interior shall conduct the internal affairs of the state administration." Article 1(3) says: "Specific internal affairs may be entrusted to other organs and organisations." And Article 7 provides that: "The minister shall determine the manner in which the Ministry of the Interior performs its duties and issues instructions for their performance." Article 9 of the Law on Internal Affairs makes reference to the "President of the Republic." Article 9 says, and I quote: "At the request of the National Assembly and the President of the Republic, the minister must submit a report on the work of the Ministry of the Interior and on the security situation in the Republic." Let's look more closely at Article 9. On its face it says: "There must be a joint and contemporaneous report of the National Assembly and the President of the Republic to submit a report to the National Assembly." Now, we say that the proper interpretation and construction of this provision is the following, and I refer back to P855, the Serbian constitution. Article 73(10), it says: "The National Assembly has the power to appoint and dismiss the president, the vice-president of the National Assembly, the prime minister, the deputy prime minister, prime ministers, and the ministers in the government." It's a power of the National Assembly. Article 94, sub 5, says: "The organisation and competencies of the ministries their departments, and special organisations shall be established by law." We've already seen that under Article 9(2) of the Serb constitution, the president has no power or authority over the National Assembly or the government and he symbolises, simply, state unity of the Republic of Serbia. There's no basis on the evidence to support this paragraph 8, subparagraph iii of the indictment. I move to paragraph 8, subparagraph iv, that says: "Mr. Milutinovic had the authority to dissolve the Republic of Serbia Assembly along with the government, 'subject to the proposal of the government on justified grounds,' although this power only applied in peacetime." I refer you, again, to the Serbian constitution, P855, Article 89. And the power to dissolve the National Assembly. 89(4), 89, subparagraph 4, says that: "This power exists in peacetime, not during a state of war, an imminent threat of war, or a state of emergency." Article 89, paragraph 1 says: "The power is divided between the government and the President of Serbia. The government must submit a proposal containing justified grounds and the President may decide to dissolve the National Assembly," again in peacetime. And Article 89, subparagraph 2 says: "If and when the National Assembly is dissolved, the government mandate ends." The conclusion, therefore, is that the National Assembly may only be dissolved in peacetime and requires a written proposal from the government to the president. I refer you further to Article 9 of the Serbian constitution. I've already mentioned subparagraph 2, but it's important to recognise the relationship between the branches of government within the Republic of Serbia. Article 9(1) says that: "Legislative power is vested in the National Assembly." Article 9(3) says: "Executive power is vested in the government." That same paragraph says: "Judicial power is vested in the courts." And as I mentioned several times already Article 9(2) says that: "State unity is symbolised through the president." That's the proper relationship, we say. Well, perhaps I have to repeat that. The transcript didn't pick up, and as I say, Article 9(3) states that: "The executive power is vested in the government and judicial power is vested in the courts of law. And the president of Serbia symbolises state unity." The reason I'm taking the Court through these sections of the indictment as a preliminary matter is because we say that throughout this indictment shows a misunderstanding and is misguided in relation to the laws and the constitutions and the legal framework in the country, and in particular, the powers and authorities that Mr. Milutinovic had as the president of Serbia. And I'm going through this in detail as well because the Chamber has heard no evidence from a witness in relation to any of this -- these constitutions or legislation. Much of the laws I'll be referring to were either tendered by the Prosecution or are the result of agreement and stipulation between the parties. I turn to two other sections of the indictment. Paragraph 8, subparagraph v, it says that: "Mr. Milutinovic, during a declared state of war or state of imminent threat of war, could enact measures normally under the competence of the Republic of Serbia, including the passage of laws; these measures could include the reorganisation of the Government and its ministries, as well as the restriction of certain rights and freedoms." And then at paragraph 35(d) of the indictment, the Prosecution alleges that Mr. Milutinovic "used his decree authority to impose measures to further the crimes charged in Counts 1, 2 and 5." We say this is another example of an incorrect and uninformed understanding of the law and the powers of the president of Serbia. Let's look at the situation during a declared state of war. The evidence in the case is that pursuant to P856 of the FRY constitution, Article 78(3): "the Federal Assembly declares a state of emergency, a state of imminent threat of war, or a state of war." According to Articles 99, subparagraphs 10 and 11 of that FRY constitution: "the Federal Government makes such a declaration, emergency, imminent threat of war, or war, if the Federal Assembly is not able to convene." Now, bearing those two of those provisions of the FRY constitution we have Exhibit P992 which is the decision to proclaim a state of imminent threat of war dated 23 March, 1999. It was proclaimed by the federal government. And the next day, on the 24th of March, P991, we have a decision to proclaim a state of war, again proclaimed by the federal government. Now, within that period of a state of war, that condition, we must turn to the Serbian constitution to see what the powers are in relation to the president of the Republic of Serbia, that's P856, Serbian constitution, Article 83, subparagraph 7. It says: "The President of the Republic shall, at his own initiative or at the proposal of the government during a state of war or immediate danger of war, pass the enactments regulating -- relating to questions falling within the competence of the National Assembly, provided he's been bound to submit them to the National Assembly for approval as soon as it is in a position to meet." Well, these provisions were in effect after the 24th of March, 1999, when the federal government declared a state of war. And during the state of war, Mr. Milutinovic, as the president of Serbia, enacted 16 decrees, each decree was enacted upon a written proposal from the government, not at his own initiative. Each of these 16 decrees was subsequently submitted to the National Assembly for approval. On the 16th of June, 1999, all 16 of these decrees were approved for the period of the state of war. And in that -- on that date, they were all declared null and void because of the cessation of the state of war. Now all 16 decrees are in evidence and the post-war decree and law ratifying those 16 decrees is in evidence. I fear I'm obliged to give you references to each one of the 16 decrees because there's no written submissions to support my submissions, so I will do so. P993 contains four decrees in the single document. The other decrees are 1D158, 1D161, 1D163, 1D166, 1D169, 1D172, 1D175, 1D178, 1D181, 1D478, 1D187, and 1D189. Those are the 16 decrees. I mention that they were all subsequently -- and each one, if you look at them, you'll see that they're expressly brought on following a written proposal from the government. Now, I told you that on the 16th of June there was a further ratification of this, of these 16 decrees, and that's 1D192, that's the law confirming the ordinance issued by the president of the republic during the state of war. The Prosecution has - and I'll just finish this section in a moment, then we can break, Your Honour - the Prosecution has tendered only four of these decrees through P993 and they seem to place special emphasis, if we can rely on the opening statement of the Prosecution, on one of them which is an ordinance on identification cards during the state of war. Well, if you look at that decree carefully, it's a decree on ID cards, saying that: "During a state of war if an ID card is lost, it must be reported." It seems that there can be nothing more understandable or natural for a state during a state of war to know who its citizens are and there's nothing criminal can be inferred from what is virtually what every other state in the world would do during a state of war. And if we turn to 1D192, the law that confirms this and every other ordinance on June 19th, 1992, under Article 2 of that law, this particular ordinance on ID cards is declared null and void. Now, it was declared null and void on the date that the state of war was abolished, and we know the state of war was abolished on the 24th of June, 1999, that's P1013, the decision of the Federal Assembly on the cessation of the state of war. So there can be no malice or malevolent intent or purpose for enacting this or any other decree. They were done according to the law on a written request by the government, ratified in June, and all the wartime decrees ceased to have any force once the state of war ended. There's nothing in any of these 16 decrees that can be said to have imposed measures to further crimes charged in Counts 1, 2, and 5 as alleged in the indictment. Your Honour, I think this might be an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before the break I was making submissions in relation to wartime decrees and in particular I was referring to the decree on ID cards. I would just add one further reference for your review, and that is Exhibit 1D226, it's the federal law on citizenship, Article 34, which provides that: "In extraordinary circumstances, such as a state of war, a citizen of the FRY cannot lose his citizenship." I turn to paragraph 7 of the indictment, which says: "On the 12 May, 1999, Sreten Lukic was promoted by decree of the President of the Republic of Serbia from Major General to Lieutenant General." On 28 May 2001, Mr. Lukic was promoted to Colonel-General by presidential decree of Mr. Milutinovic. There is no evidence in this case to support that allegation. Paragraph 36(j), Milan Milutinovic's "failure to exercise his powers as President of Serbia to prevent the perpetration and/or to punish the perpetrators, of crimes charged in this indictment." There is no evidence of any de jure or de facto powers as the president of Serbia conferred upon Mr. Milutinovic to do any of those things and no material ability to do them either. I'd like to address the Chamber on two central tenets on the allegations against Mr. Milutinovic and those regard the Supreme Defence Council and the Supreme Command. The relevant parts or portions of the indictment are paragraph 8, paragraph 2; paragraph 23; paragraph 35, subparagraphs (a), (b), and (e); paragraph 36, subparagraphs (a) and (b); and paragraph 38. Prosecution alleges that Mr. Milutinovic was a member of the Supreme Defence Council and the Supreme Command and that during a state of war the Supreme Command had authority over the VJ and other organisations engaged in the defence of the FRY. I propose to review the following evidence: The constitutions; relevant legislation, which is the law on the VJ and the Law on Defence; minutes of the Supreme Defence Council; the rules of procedure of the Supreme Defence Council; and the testimony of Prosecution witnesses. First, the constitution of the FRY, P856. According to Articles 133 to 138 of the constitution, the VJ is a federal army. Articles 135 and 136 refer to the powers of the president of the FRY and it also refers to the Supreme Defence Council. Under Article 135, it states that: "The federal President, the President of the FRY, commands the VJ in wartime and in peacetime in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council." I'll be returning later in my submissions to the meaning of the phrase "in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council." The same section, 135, stipulates that the Supreme Defence Council is made up of the President of FRY, the President of Serbia, the President of Montenegro, and that the federal president presides over the Supreme Defence Council. Article 136 of the FRY constitution reads as follows: "The President of the Republic," that's the federal republic, "shall appoint, promote, and dismiss from service officers of the Army of Yugoslavia stipulated by federal law; shall appoint and dismiss the president, judges and judge assessors of military tribunals and military prosecutors." I mention that there are two relevant federal laws that we must review: They are P984, the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, 1994; and P985, the Law on Defence, 1994. The first thing I think the Chamber should be aware of is that the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, is an ex officio member of the Supreme Defence Council. Indeed, both the president of the Republic of Montenegro and the president of Serbia are ex officio, pursuant to Article 135 of the federal constitution. The republic constitutions of both Montenegro and Serbia are silent on the matter. So by virtue of holding the office of president of Serbia, the federal constitution provides that the president of Serbia is a member of the Supreme Defence Council. Now, earlier this morning I said that we had to reconcile, from time to time, the Serbian constitution of 1990 with the FRY constitution of 1992, and here's another example of that. The Republic of Serbia has never had armed forces. Until 1992, the federal army was the JNA in the federal state known as the SFRY. During the indictment period and since 1992, the federal army is the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ. Now, if one were to look at the Serbian constitution, P855, Article 83(4), we find this provision: "The President of the Republic," the Republic of Serbia, "shall command the armed forces in peacetime and in wartime and the popular resistance in war, order the general and partial mobilisation, organise the preparations for defence in accordance with law." Now, we've seen and I've made submissions on the paramountcy argument, but there's even more specific legislation in place. I refer you to 1D456 which is a 1991 Law on Ministries which created the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia, 1991. Well, that ministry was abolished in 1993 by 1D142 which is the law correcting and amending the Law on Ministries. And all ministries whose activities fell under federal jurisdiction were abolished by this law, including the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia. So again, as the SFRY broke up and the nascent state of FRY found its way between 1990 and 1992 and the early 1990s, we see that there are perhaps not perfect reconciliation between the two constitutions, Serbia and FRY, but we do have the paramountcy clauses and we do have, in this instance, legislation which corrects what would appear on the face of it to be an anomaly and Serbia never had armed forces. Our submission is that the VJ is commanded by the president of the FRY, he is the Supreme Commander. On the principle of singleness of command and unity of the command, it's the Supreme Commander who commands the forces, it's not commanded by a collegiate group. The Supreme Defence Council, it performed a function of national defence, and we say this is borne out by a review of the law, the minutes of the meetings, and the evidence of witnesses. I've referred you already to Articles 135 and 136 of the FRY constitution which says, 135 says: "In wartime and peacetime, the Army of Yugoslavia shall be under the command of the President of the Republic in accordance with decisions by the Supreme Defence Council." And 136 refers specifically to promotions, appointments, and dismissals in the VJ. In our submission, the Law on the VJ as implementing legislation, that's P984, sets out the powers and authority of the federal president and his command authority over the VJ. I wish to read out Article 4 of that law to you. It says: "The President of the Republic shall command the army in war and peace in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council." It picks up the language of Article 135 of the federal constitution. It goes on to say: "In his command of the army, the President of the Republic," the federal president, "shall," and there are eight items he shall do: "The president of the republic shall establish the principles of organisation, the development and equipping of the army;" Subparagraph 2: "Determine the system of command in the army and oversee its implementation." Subparagraph 3: "Decide on the deployment of the army and approve the plan for its use;" Subparagraph 4: "Regulate and order readiness of the army in case of imminent threat of war, state of war, or state of emergency;" Subparagraph 5: "Provide guide-lines for arrangements relating to mobilisation and issue orders for the mobilisation of the army;" Subparagraph 6: "Issue basic regulations and other acts related to the deployment of the army;" Subparagraph 7: "Adopt rules regulating the internal order and relations in the performance of military service;" And subparagraph 8: "Perform other duties relating to the command over the army in accordance with federal law." And what of the power of the federal president to promote, appoint, and dismiss? We invite the Chamber to consider these sections - and I'll just enumerate them - of the Law on the VJ: Article 16, 28, 46, 107, 151, 204, 208, 291, 296, 316, and 318. All of those articles I have just enumerated grant express power to the federal president to promote, appoint, and dismiss. He is the commander of the VJ. What does the Law on Defence tell us? That's P985, I refer you to Article 40 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry for interruption. I have a question. Now, he's the commander, that means Commander-in-Chief. Well, then he acts on the advice of a defence council.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Where would you differentiate between as far as when he acts as the Commander-in-Chief, and when he acts on the advice of the defence council because he is subject to that? I mean, just a differentiation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect there is no differentiation to make: He is the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Then he acts on the advice of -- if defence council -- defence council states that this is to be explored and not this; go this way or do that way. As far as the battle-field, then he doesn't go for the battle-field. Somebody else is going.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm just about to address that in my submission because I think when we see the Law on Defence in particular and the minutes of the meetings, we see that it's an advisory panel that deals with national defence and not the army. And the true nature, both in law and in fact, will come out with a review of the legislation, and the minutes, the agenda, what's discussed, and what's decided and the way it's decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I just referred the Chamber to P985, which is the piece of federal legislation, the Law on Defence. And I begin with Article 40 which deals with the rights and duties of the federal president. Article 40 again picks up on the language of Article 135 of the federal constitution. It reads: "In accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, the President of the Republic:" Subparagraph 1: "Orders implementation of the country's defence plan, commands the Army of Yugoslavia in wartime and peacetime, and decides on the country's territorial division into military areas." Those are the first three paragraphs of Article 40. Article 40, subparagraph 1, referred to a defence plan. Article 85 of this Law on Defence deals with the defence plan and the Supreme Defence Council was to issue a defence plan, a plan for the defence of the country within six months of the day this law comes into force, which was in 1994. Now I turn to Article 41 of the Law on Defence, and I believe at this point I'll start addressing the question posed to me a moment ago by Judge Chowhan. Article 41 on the Law on Defence sets out eight subparagraphs in relation to the Supreme Defence Council. And I'll quote this section in its entirety again. "The Supreme Defence Council:" Subparagraph 1: "Adopts the country's defence plan." Subparagraph 2: "Renders decisions in accordance with which the President of the Republic commands the Army of Yugoslavia." Subparagraph 3: "Assesses possible war and other dangers to the defence and security of the country." Subparagraph 4: "Determines the equipment and weapons needed for the country's defence." Subparagraph 5: "Determines the arrangement of the territory for the country's defence." Subparagraph 6: "Determines the strategy of armed conflict and the rules on the use of force in the country's defence and the conduct of war." Subparagraph 7: "Approves the basic elements, training plans, and programme for the country's defence and preparation for work in areas relating to the country's defence." Now, when I turn to -- now to reviewing the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council, which are in evidence, I ask the Chamber to bear in mind the language and the powers conferred on the Supreme Defence Council by Article 41. It deals with the country's defence, it makes assessments, it makes determinations, it provides counsel to the Commander-in-Chief, the president of the federal republic. And not to get ahead of myself, I submit that when we go through the minutes of the meeting, which I intend to do right now, that will be borne out. First I will enumerate the minutes of the meeting which are in evidence: P1573 is the 3rd Session of the Supreme Defence Council, 24 December 1997; P1574 is the 5th Session of the Supreme Defence Council, 9 June 1998; P1575 is the 6th Session of the Supreme Defence Council, 4 October 1998; P1576 is the 7th Session of the Supreme Defence Council, 24 November 1998; P1000 is the 8th Session of the Supreme Defence Council, 25 December 1998; and P1577 is the 9th Session of the Supreme Defence Council, 23 March 1999. Two sets of the rules of procedure of the Supreme Defence Council are in evidence, they are 2622 -- P2622, the rules of procedure from 23 July 1992; and P1738, the rules of procedure from 23 March 1999. Now, I've asked the Chamber to bear in mind the language of Article 41 on the Law on Defence, and I would also invite the Chamber to simply peruse the - as a starting point - the agendas of each of the meetings I've just described to you. What sort of matters are brought before the Supreme Defence Council? On what issues are decisions brought, in accordance with which the president of the FRY commands the army? Well, it deals with personnel issues, the 5th -- at the 5th Session, for example, there was a discussion on the military and political situation in the region and the situation at the state border with the Republic of Albania. Matters dealing with the military budget are discussed. You'll see when you review these minutes that there's the issue of Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro making contributions to the military budget. Financing comes up a lot. Personnel matters comes up a lot. In December there's information given on candidates for the post in the Army of Yugoslavia to be decided by the president of the FRY. On 23rd of March, 1999, on the eve of the war there's a discussion on the current military and political situation in the region, and danger of NATO aggression against the FRY. So we say that even the -- as a preliminary step, a perusal of the types of matters and issues brought before the Supreme Defence Council supports our contention that this is an advisory body. But let's go further, let's look at the details. I would take you first to the 5th Session of the Supreme Defence Council on the 9th of June, 1998, P1574. There the agenda has two items: Personnel issues and the second item is interpretation of the present military and political situation in the region and the situation at the state border to the Republic of Albania. I remind you we're in June 1998. Now, General Perisic is present at this meeting, and when you review his report to the Supreme Defence Council, he talks about the level of danger facing the FRY from the vicinity. He talks about from the Italian territory, from Macedonia, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, terrorist training camps in Albania, and the conclusion, unanimous conclusion, reached by the three presidents is threefold. First, the report by the Chief of Staff is hereby accepted - I'm at page 3 of this exhibit. The second conclusion: Should terrorist activities of the Albanian separatist movement escalate, the Army of Yugoslavia will intervene appropriately; and the third part of this decision is, conclusion: The Army of Yugoslavia will be prepared to oppose any form of foreign intervention that can endanger the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia. We say this is an example of the nature of discussion, the nature of this body, the Supreme Defence Council. Information is provided, discussions are held, assessments are made, views are expressed and exchanged, and this body is dealing with national defence. We say it's an advisory body and an advisory body to the president of the FRY who commands the VJ as the Supreme Commander. The examples I've just given you of the conclusions or the decisions are spelled out in the broadest terms, general declarations, general findings, based on the power conferred on the Supreme Defence Council by the law. And I'll proceed to the next several meetings and I submit that you will see that as we go through the year 1998 and up to 1999 that this is, in fact, the way this body functioned, as I've just described. The 6th Session, 4 October 1998, P1575. One item on the agenda, which is the interpretation of the present military and political situation in the region. The context is UN Security Council Resolution 1199, that's Exhibit P456. Again, General Perisic is there and he transmits an assessment that was made by the General Staff of the VJ. He says that the present military and political issues in the region deal with the defence capabilities of the FRY, an assessment of a NATO attack by air, sea, and land. He says that the General Staff came to the general consensus that to ensure peace there should be full compliance with UN Resolution 1119 [sic], that a peaceful solution through dialogue and political means should be sought, but that the country should defend itself if attacked. Now, Mr. Milutinovic spoke at this meeting and at page 4 I'll quote what he said. The minutes record that: "The President of the Republic of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic, agreed with the assessment of the military and political situation which General Perisic had presented with regard to NATO forces, but expressed the hope that reason would, however, prevail and there would be no strikes. But if the whole of the US [sic] Resolution was examined point by point -- UN Resolution was examined point by point, we have practically done everything. If we need to do something more, then let us do it to avoid strikes. However, if despite everything we are attacked, we will have to be prepared to the utmost, we have to defend the country." On pages 7 and 8, President Milosevic stated four points that flowed from this meeting. The first point is the suspension of combat operations. Remember, we're in October 1998 and there was the suspension of the fighting at that time. We're just on the eve of the Milosevic-Holbrooke KVM agreement. Second: "The withdrawal of forces to the permanent stations in proportion to the suspension of terrorist activities which is part of our agreement with President Yeltsin of Russia." We have evidence in this case that in mid-June there was the Yeltsin-Milosevic agreement which brought KDOM and ECMM to the territory. Third: "The opening of the entire area for free movement by representatives of the UNHCR and the International Red Cross in order to help resolve the humanitarian problems." And four: "Our readiness for dialogue and the peaceful resolution of problems." And what's the conclusion of the Supreme Defence Council, what is its decision? It's this, a unanimous decision: "Yugoslavia is firmly in favour of peace and ready to resolve all open questions by peaceful means, but if the country is attacked we shall defend ourselves with all possible means." That's a decision on the Supreme Defence Council in accordance with which the federal president, Mr. Milosevic, commanded the VJ. I move to the 7th Session of the Supreme Defence Council, 24 November 1998, P1576. Two items on the agenda: A review of the military budget for 1999 and personnel issues. The only relevance or importance, I would say, in relation to the budgetary issue is that we see the beginnings of the problems that were existing between Montenegro and the FRY. You'll see, when you review this -- these minutes, that President Djukanovic is informed and reminded that Montenegro's not paying its fair share into the military budget. We also know, we have evidence here from witnesses that in later meetings Mr. Djukanovic was being obstructive at the VS Supreme Defence Council and indeed, he stopped coming to meetings. Personnel issues, here the issue of replacing the Chief of the General Staff and filling the vacancy of the air force and anti-aircraft defence commander. President Milosevic proposed the replacement of Colonel-General Perisic, and he puts forward two names: Colonel-General Velickovic and Colonel-General Ojdanic. And the reasons put forward for Mr. Milosevic for replacing General Perisic are at page 3 that: "Perisic has been in the post for an uncommonly long period." President Milosevic says: "In the future the Chief of the General Staff should not hold the post so long, stating the example of the USA, where three generals held the post in the past five years." President Milosevic also points out that: "Mr. Perisic has been appointed advisor to the federal government on defence issues and after a transformation of the federal ministry, and the General Staff he may even be destined to become the federal minister of defence." Now, in this meeting you'll see that President Djukanovic is opposed to replacing General Perisic. He supports the re-organisation of the General Staff, he supports the re-organisation of the federal Ministry of Defence. He's opposed to replacing Perisic, he says, because length of time as chief of staff is not a factor. "In his view Perisic is a proven authority with great experience, good cooperation with Montenegro, defends the interests of the VJ at home and abroad, and he's better prepared for the position than the other candidates." Mr. Milutinovic makes this observation at page 4, and I quote, "President Milutinovic had a different opinion with regard to the issue of replacing the superior officer of the General Staff, although he does not contest what President Djukanovic said." He pointed out that: "We need a Chief of General Staff who is an excellent operative. At the international level, General Perisic acted in accordance with political instructions of legitimate organs of this country's political government. That was undoubtedly successful. Nevertheless he has been holding that post for a long time and a change should be made. We now have parallel institutions in the General Staff and the federal Ministry of Defence, SMO, and doubling of some activities which is evidently uneconomical and expensive." Mr. Milutinovic goes on to say: "As for the good opinion others have of Perisic at the international level, that should be taken with a grain of salt and we shouldn't pay much attention to that. We will settle our internal affairs as we think best and not according to their interests. General Ojdanic is less well known to the general public, perhaps, but he is not less excellent in comparison with the present Chief of Staff." Then there is an exchange between President Milosevic and President Djukanovic which ties in to Articles 135 and 136 of the federal constitution and the powers of the president and the role of the Supreme Defence Council. President Djukanovic says this in relation to his opposition to replacing Colonel-General Perisic. I quote at page 5: "The response to that, President Djukanovic again insisted that they establish that the president of Montenegro expressed a negative opinion with regard to replacing the Chief of Staff of the VJ, Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic. He then went on to say that the regulations regarding jurisdiction over the army are clear, that it is not good that the earlier practice in the work and decision-making process of the Supreme Defence Council is being abandoned." How does President Milosevic respond to that? He invokes Articles 135 and 136 of the federal constitution. And this is the crux of the point in our submission. At page 5, "President Milosevic pointed out that he was satisfied with the manner of debate at the session of the Supreme Defence Council. Despite some differences. The debate was constructive and correct. He also reminded council members that according to the constitution of the SR Yugoslavia, decisions on the appointments of generals are issued by the president of the republic." President Milosevic said: "According to the constitution the jurisdiction of the president of the republic in relation to the Army of Yugoslavia is regulated in two articles." He refers to 135 and 136. He says, "In one it says" - in my submission, he is referring to 135 - "in one it says that the President of the Republic commands the army in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council," and then it says who are the members and who the president of the Supreme Defence Council is. This article pertains to the use of the army. A standpoint is adopted about it at the council and authorities are transferred on to direct executives such as, for instance, the engagement of additional forces in Kosmet, Kosovo and Metohija. Then President Milosevic refers to Article 136 of the constitution. In the next 136th article of the constitution: "Jurisdiction of the President of the Republic are regulated in the appointment and discharge of generals, military court judges, military prosecutors, and their deputies in accordance with the federal law. This is the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia in which the jurisdiction of the President of the Republic are further specified." Then President Milosevic explains that he will seek the opinion and consult members of the VSO, but the final decisions are his. He says, "President Milosevic noted that until recently the practice and the work of the Supreme Defence Council was to put many issues on the agenda and that the federal government and other organs can decide about. The council's opinion was sought even for matters that are exclusively and constitutionally in the jurisdiction of the president of the republic. "Concluding the debate, the President said he would always in the future consult members of the Supreme Defence Council, presidents of the member republics, about the most important issues pertaining to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But then, sorry for interruption, now we know what is consultation. One is a consultation which has a binding effect. One is a consult -- and this has been discussed in various constitutions. One is an advice which has a binding effect and one is an advice that's just advice and like ether, it goes away. But when you talk of consultation here, now things are becoming different here, when he may consult but he may follow his own views. I mean, this requires a bit of elucidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I think you find the answer to that, Your Honour, when you look in the rules of procedure and the -- who calls the meetings and the agenda and what -- what is or what is not put on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough then in showing from the minutes of the meeting how all this took a shape and how the president was bound or was he not bound or whether he overruled or whether he did this because in appointments he had the absolute power. Consultation can be just a consultation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- the answer, in my submission, is - and I'll come -- perhaps I'm getting ahead of myself but I will answer the question. It is the phrase: "In accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council." What we must look at is what in fact was on the agenda and if a matter is not -- if there's no decision by the Supreme Defence Council, then there's nothing in accordance with which the federal president has his discretion or powers fettered. In other words, if we look at factually which matters are brought before this body, they deal with personnel, they deal with information, they deal with consultations and assessments. Now, if -- if the agenda, in fact, did include a whole array of other things, command and control and anything else, then perhaps then it can be argued. But we must look at exactly what took place and what -- and the way in which President Milosevic understood Articles 135 and 136. And the next meeting of the Supreme Defence Council, I believe, expands a bit on that again. Because here we see president -- President Djukanovic questioning or opposing an appointment and President Milosevic invoking 135 and 136 of the FRY constitution. And in the next meeting in December we have a further exchange between President Milosevic and President Djukanovic. But I think we cannot sit back in the abstract and limit ourselves to the language of the constitution or the law on the VJ and the law on the Defence. We must look as well at what is the nature of the body in practice, what matters are brought before this body and the tone of discussions, the nature of the conclusions, all of which, in our submission, are there -- it's there as a consultative body. That's -- and that's what President Milosevic is saying, that he would seek the opinion of members and he would consult with them. The 8th Session of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suppose, Mr. O'Sullivan, as long as he had Mr. Milutinovic agreeing with him generally, it really didn't matter very much what Djukanovic thought and what, strictly speaking, the constitution said.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, that is a comment that can be made, I would say, if you divorce yourself from what exactly was discussed or what was brought before this body. And the specific question of promotions is expressly granted to the federal president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the comment by Milosevic was wider when he said, "On important matters from now on I will consult, but I will make the decisions." And that statement's consistent with Djukanovic saying, Well, we're departing from previous practice. But if you've got the power by majority you can depart from the previous practice, whatever the rules say. So there's a de facto situation to be dealt with also, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the de facto situation, in my submission, is dealt with by the very nature of the matters that are brought before this body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I move to the 8th Session in December 1998, which is P1000. There the agenda has three matters: A discussion on the situation of the state border with the Republic of Albania; financing of the VJ in 1999; and a report on the proposed appointments in the VJ submitted for decision to the president of the FRY. Now, the discussion on the situation at the state border is dealt with in a report by General Ojdanic, who at this point is the chief of staff, and he's reporting on the border between the FRY-Albania-Macedonia. He's reporting on illegal border crossings from those neighbouring countries between January and December 1998 and all the problems that's causing in the sector of the Pristina Corps. In our submission, there's nothing particularly relevant to the discussion on financing, and on the promotions and appointments, President Milosevic says that it's a year-end, it's the tradition time for promotions and appointments and the cessation of service and he requests comments, suggests, and remarks about those appointments and again President Djukanovic says that he notes that this is for information purposes only and notification and that the decision is made by the president of the FRY. At page 9, President Djukanovic said that: "This item of the agenda came under the heading of information, which means that it's only presented for the council's notification, but that it is not decided upon by the council but by the president of FRY. However, in his opinion, the other participants at the session should have the possibility to give their opinions on the matter in the discussion, regardless of the distribution of authority which is as it is." We've heard evidence in this trial in relation to P1000, these minutes of the Supreme Defence Council. And it's at this point when this was shown to General Vasiljevic and General Vasiljevic, both in this trial and in the Milosevic trial, pointed out that at this point it was common knowledge that President Djukanovic was being obstructionist and, indeed, that was the position of his evidence in Milosevic. The Prosecution knew that, and they adduced it from him in this trial as well, and in fact, that testimony in Milosevic is an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This would also be consistent with the idea that Djukanovic was continuing his protest but now he's trying to restore the right to be consulted, having lost the right to participate in the decision and the agenda heading simply says "notification" now. So he's expressing the view that he's not even being consulted anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the rules of procedure don't say that. President Djukanovic can propose an agenda or items for the agenda; there's no complaint about that. And of course we're not -- we are not here to debate anything other than whether or not there's proof beyond a reasonable doubt that this body is, as the Prosecution alleges, in command of the VJ and forces of the country. And we're saying, well, if there's all these different interpretations, surely, surely, the innocent one must be adopted for Mr. Milutinovic. When we look at the totality of the evidence of the constitution, the laws, the nature of the debates, the tone of the debates, the agendas, and the voting as -- in these meetings. The Prosecution's taken the position that when President Milosevic says that there's nothing irregular about the use of the Pristina Corps, that's page 8651 of our transcript, the Prosecution, during the testimony of General Vasiljevic, the Prosecution has taken the position that Mr. Milosevic is lying to the other members of the Supreme Defence Council when he says there were no complaints domestically or abroad, because he was withholding the information of the letter that General Perisic sent to him in July. If that's the Prosecution's position, I make no further comment on it. But what are the conclusions of this meeting? Again, what's the decision? It's a unanimous decision and there are -- it's threefold. "First, in Kosovo and Metohija, the Yugoslav Army operated in accordance with the rules of service. The Pristina Corps carried out its tasks very successfully; Two, for personnel to have better conditions to protect the border, that is, in order to increase the length of individual border stretches under control, it is necessary to build new border posts, especially along the border with Albania, provide an adequate boat on Lake Skadar for securing the border running through the lake; and 3, the Supreme Defence Council will continue to be apprised of all matters regarding the army and all remarks shall be discussed and taken into account in the decision-making process." And the last minutes I wish to discuss with you are P1577, the 9th Session on the 23rd of March, 1999. President Djukanovic is not present. The agenda has two items. The first is consideration of the current military-political situation in the region and the danger of a NATO aggression on the FRY, and the second point is consideration of the rules of procedure of the Supreme Defence Council. Clearly we're on the eve of the -- of the war and the threat of a NATO attack against the FRY. At page 2, Mr. Milutinovic made this observation: "The President of the Republic, Milan Milutinovic, especially emphasised that our delegation in Rambouillet did everything in its power to find a peaceful solution to the problem in Kosovo and Metohija but that the west had obviously decided to mark the 50th anniversary of the formation of NATO in a spectacular manner and considering everything, it is ready to as soon as tomorrow carry out an aggression against our country from the sea and air." What are the conclusions on this point of the agenda? What's the decision? Page 2: "Concluding the debate regarding the first item on the agenda President Milosevic pointed out the realistic threat of aggression and recalled the stand presented early in October 1998 at a session of the Supreme Defence Council, VSO, that the FRY would do everything to find a peaceful solution to the problem in Kosovo, but if we should be attacked we shall defend the country with all means." That's the decision taken on the eve of the war in accordance with which president of the FRY commanded the VJ. The same conclusion that had been arrived at in October 1998. There's also consideration in the adoption of new rules of procedure for the Supreme Defence Council at pages 2 and 3, it says: "The council considered the innovative text of the rules of the procedure of the Supreme Defence Council. The participants of the session stated that the text of the rules of procedure provided conditions for the efficient work of the sessions of the VSO, Supreme Defence Council, and adoption of its decisions." In our submission, we see the real nature and power of the Supreme Defence Council through the constitutions, legislation, and the minutes. Under Article 135, the president -- the federal president in wartime and peace commands the army in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. There's one commander who's the president of the FRY, the Supreme Commander, based on the principle of unity and singleness of command. We see that in 1998 there were, in fact, four meetings of the Supreme Defence Council, minutes of three of those meetings are in evidence. One meeting in 1999 on the 23rd of March. And there's no evidence of any further meeting of the Supreme Defence Council thereafter, and particularly not during the indictment period after the 23rd of March, 1999. What does the phrase "in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council" mean? I've asked the Court to look at the practice as reflected in the minutes. Look at the nature of the topics and the matters brought before the Supreme Defence Council for decision. They are entirely consistent with Article 41 of the Law on Defence, information, discussion, advice; no command authority, no issues of command are ever raised or discussed. The Supreme Defence Council did not meet during the war, as I said. P1738 are the rules of procedure adopted on the 23rd of March, 1999. It increases the quorum, to have the three presidents along with the minister of defence and the chief of general staff present to constitute a quorum of the Supreme Defence Council. We say that the Supreme Defence Council plays no role in commanding the VJ or other forces. The presidents of the republics, Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Djukanovic, play no role in commanding the armed forces. It's a federal army. The declaration of war is a federal act. It's federal jurisdiction, declared by the federal government, the minister of defence is federal; the Commander-in-Chief is the federal president commanding the federal army in a time of war. That's both the legal and factual analysis that shows that the Supreme Defence Council is not the body that the Prosecution alleges that it is. Let me now turn to the evidence, and the evidence here of course is quite scant, isn't it, Your Honours? The only person who was brought to this court who can speak to these issues was General Vasiljevic. Our submission, he's not qualified to give evidence in relation to the Supreme Defence Council. He retired from the JNA in 1992, in May 1992. The constitution of the FRY came into force on the 27th of April, 1992, weeks before his retirement. In the transcript at 8642, General Vasiljevic said he was not familiar with the constitution, and when he was reinstated in April 1999, he says he did not read the constitution, and furthermore he can offer no expertise at all in relation to the constitutions, regulations, and laws. But what did General Vasiljevic tell you? He spoke about the Supreme Commander and the Supreme Command Staff during the war. You'll note that General Vasiljevic was an assistant to General Farkas who was a member of the General Staff of the VJ. That's the position General Vasiljevic assumed in 1999. General Vasiljevic said the General Staff becomes the Staff of the Supreme Command, and he said that there was a -- yes, General Farkas was a member of the General Staff of the VJ. When asked directly by the Prosecution, General Vasiljevic says that the Supreme Commander was President Milosevic and the Supreme Commander gave direction to the army through the command staff. The Supreme Commander refers to the individual who was giving direction to the VJ through the General Staff. He said that in his testimony here; He said it in P2600, which is his OTP interview, paragraphs 15 and 16; he said it in P2589, which is his testimony in Milosevic beginning on page 15964. General Vasiljevic said the reports went up the vertical chain of command. The Staff of [Realtime transcript read in error "and"] the Supreme Command reported to President Milosevic as the Supreme Commander. We ask you also to consider -- yes, line 18 should be the Staff of the Supreme Command reported to President Milosevic as the Supreme Commander. We ask you also to consider a number of contemporaneous exhibits, a publication, which has been entered into evidence by agreement, the Vojska magazine. The first edition I refer you to was 1D459, dated 27 March 1999. It's a short article written to explain the legal consequences and mechanisms during a state of war, what happens. It talks about the -- Mr. Milosevic, the federal president being the Commander-in-Chief; describes the presidential powers; describes the state of war; and there's no reference to the president of Serbia or Supreme Command. 1D460 is the 5th of April, 1999, President Milosevic is referred to as the president of the republic and Supreme Commander when he meets Mr. Rugova; 1D461, 7th of April, again President Milosevic as the Supreme Commander; 1D462, 10th of April, 1999, President Milosevic, the president and the Supreme Commander receives representatives from Greece, Russia, and Hungary; 1D463, 14th of April, 1999, President Milosevic, the Supreme Commander, receives foreign representatives; 1D467, 29 April 1999, President Milosevic, Commander-in-Chief, receives congratulations on FRY day, 28th of April, 1999; 1D468, 10th of May, both President Milosevic and President Milutinovic are mentioned in this article. President Milosevic is the president and the Supreme Commander who receives a Greek delegation. President Milutinovic, the president of the Republic of Serbia, receives the same Greek delegation. He's described only as the president of the Republic of Serbia. Your Honours, there's no evidence in this case that Mr. Milutinovic was a member of a body called the Supreme Command. The Prosecution cannot point to even the existence of a body called the Supreme Command. The evidence is that there was a supreme commander, who was the president of the FRY; the evidence is that the Supreme Defence Council did not meet; Mr. Milutinovic had no role in any of the allegations as set out and alleged by the Prosecution in its indictment. Let me turn now to 1998 and the acts and conduct of Mr. Milutinovic and his state of mind, as reflected in the Prosecution's evidence. We all know very well that there's been very little evidence heard in this court in relation to Mr. Milutinovic during the Prosecution's case. The evidence is nothing short of scant. There's absolutely no evidence of any criminal intent or criminal conduct by Mr. Milutinovic. Let's look first at P455 which is a UN Resolution 1160, 31st of March, 1998. There the Security Council is talking about the best way to defeat terrorism in Kosovo, to offer the Kosovar Albanians a genuine political process. It calls on the leadership in Belgrade and of the Kosovar Albanians to meet for meaningful dialogue. It calls on granting substantial -- a substantial degree of greater autonomy and meaningful self-administration to Kosovo. And it refers to the education agreement and declaration made by Mr. Milutinovic on the 18th of March, 1998. That declaration by Mr. Milutinovic is 1D79, 18th of March, 1998. Mr. Milutinovic calls for immediate political dialogue between the representatives of the Government of Serbia and the Albanian leaders. Mr. Milutinovic holds himself out as a guarantor of these discussions based on territorial integrity and self-government for Kosovo and Metohija within Serbia. He makes an appeal for seeking dialogue, peaceful methods, and political means. Mr. Milutinovic calls for the implementation of the education agreement, and he says at one point: "I point out my conviction that the future of the citizens in Kosovo and Metohija as one of those -- as well as those in Serbia and in all of our country does not lie in ethnic, religious, or cultural closing-up and divisions, but in peace, equality, integration, and life together." Now, what's the context of this resolution and Mr. Milutinovic's speech? Well, we have exhibits to that effect, 1D78 is a statement by the Government of Serbia on the 11th of March, 1998, which creates a state delegation headed by Deputy Prime Minister Ratko Markovic. You'll know that Professor Markovic eventually leads the state delegation to Rambouillet, but we're in March 1998. The second important exhibit is 1D18, e-court pages 90 and 91, it's the agreement on measures on education where there had been agreement for the re-opening of the Institute of Albanology, the re-opening of the university faculties in Pristina with future plans to open more faculties, opening elementary schools, high schools. The next exhibit is 1D82, again a statement by the Government of Serbia, 31 March, 1998. It expands the Markovic state delegation to include minorities, including Albanians from Kosovo, in that delegation. It also includes Professor Kutlesic, who at that time was one of the deputy prime ministers of the federal government who was a Special Envoy to President Milosevic to take part in that committee and meet and try to reach a peaceful, meaningful solution to the problems in Kosovo. Not to belabour the point that I made earlier this morning about Article 9(2) of the Serb constitution, but the speech and undertaking by Mr. Milutinovic is consistent with his role as the symbol of unity for the Republic of Serbia. He's holding himself out as a guarantor, making himself available for this process, speaking on behalf of all citizens of Serbia, calling on the Albanian leadership to enter into dialogue. His acts and conduct and state of mind here are consistent with the powers of the president of Serbia and in no way suggest any malevolence or criminal intent. We know that on the 7th of April, 1998, President Milutinovic travels to Kosovo and Metohija with the delegation headed by Professor Markovic to meet the Albanian leaders who did not appear for the meeting. On that occasion, 1D83, President Milutinovic makes a statement, 7th of April, 1998, he says that the future of all citizens of Kosovo and Metohija and Serbia and the whole country is not in ethnic division or cessation but in equality and well-linked mutual life. He calls on continued dialogue despite the refusal of leadership and again he pledges that he himself is ready to meet at any moment in Belgrade whenever the representatives of the Albanian political parties decide to do so. Now, Ambassador Petritsch was here. You know that he was the Austrian Ambassador to Yugoslavia and the EU Special Envoy on Kosovo. He was aware of these speeches by Mr. Milutinovic. He knew that he was making repeated efforts to encourage the Kosovo Albanian representatives to meet with the Markovic delegation. I'm referring to pages 1075 -- 10785 to 10788. He knew that Mr. Milutinovic was critical of the Albanians for not appearing when invited, and that Mr. Milutinovic kept emphasising the importance of this issue to Serbia to find the solution, a resolution to the problem in 1998, and that was one of his key objectives and an objective of the Serbian government. Professor -- Ambassador Petritsch also was aware of the fact that in the spring of 1998, 12 to 15 different invitations, coming either from the government, Professor Markovic, and at times from Mr. Milutinovic, were ignored by the Albanian majority leadership. Now, you've also heard evidence that this whole problem of Kosovo became internationalised in mid-June with the Yeltsin-Milosevic Agreement. Ambassador Byrnes and Ambassador Petritsch spoke about that, that's 1D18, 289, that brought KDOM and ECMM to the mission. Ambassador Petritsch -- The Yeltsin-Milosevic agreement is 1D18, page 289. My apologies. This brought international involvement to Kosovo and Metohija, with constructive rule on the part of Russia. It brought freedom of movement to accredited diplomats, access by humanitarian organisations, state assistance to rebuild homes. There's also evidence in the case of visits to Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 by Mr. Milutinovic. One such visit was the 23rd of September, 1998. Several witnesses have testified about events relevant to that visit, we say. Dr. Dunjic was a pathologist who autopsied bodies at Radonjic Lake; John Crosland was a British military attache who visited Radonjic Lake and observed the bodies; Zlatomir Pesic was a VJ officer who attended this meeting on the 23rd of September; as was Ljubinko Cvetic, a MUP officer who attended that meeting. We say that the visit by Mr. Milutinovic occurred on the 23rd of September, 1998, shortly after the times of the killings at Radonjic Lake, which at the time were believed to be killings committed by the KLA. Mr. Pesic and Mr. Cvetic were present at the meeting. The evidence of Mr. Pesic is, and that's P2502, his supplemental information and transcript, 7215, 7217, his evidence is that Mr. Milutinovic was a guest of the MUP in a small hall where attendees sat in rows. He sat in the fourth row. Mr. Milutinovic and General Lukic sat at a front table. Mr. Milutinovic addressed the group on the political and security situation in Serbia and how it reflected on the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. Mr. Cvetic gives a similar account of that meeting, that's transcript 8189, Cvetic, yes. He recalls that Mr. Milutinovic said that terrorism had been defeated, the conditions for resolving problems in Kosovo and Metohija by a peaceful means had been created, that only minority terrorist groups remained, the security situation would improve, and everyone should work in line to help resolve the problems. What other evidence is there of activities of Mr. Milutinovic in 1998? We know that on the 14th of October, he attended a meeting of the Government of Serbia, that's P656, Serbian government endorses accord reached by President Milosevic, that's the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreements. Mr. Milutinovic reported to the Serbian government on the talks held between President Milosevic and Richard Holbrooke. He informed them of the -- that the talks lasted over several days and that a definite accord had been reached solving problems in Kosovo and Metohija in a peaceful way by political means. He presented this report to the government, and in particular the 11 points that flowed from the agreement between Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Milosevic and a timetable. You have Exhibit 1D204, which is a copy of those 11 points and timetable, which was submitted to the UN Security Council by the FRY at the time. Now, we are in early October. You know that there's Exhibit 1D202, the conclusions of the National Assembly of Serbia, 28 September condemning terrorism; distinguishing between terrorists and Albanian people; and condemning terrorist support from the Republic of Albania; calling for dialogue, immediate continuation of dialogue; democratic resolution of the problem; equality among Serbs, Montenegrins, Albanians, Turks, Muslims, Roma, and others; and that the future of Kosovo and Metohija was not to be built on ethnic, religious, or cultural divisions. The list of people mentioned in this conclusion of the Serbian Assembly should also include Albanians along with all the others. You also have evidence, Your Honours, of what we've called the Hill process, draft agreements which are 1D18 exhibits, prepared by Ambassador Hill with the collaboration of Ambassador Petritsch on October 1st, November 1st, and December 2nd. Well, 1D86 and P556 are two documents which give an account of a meeting chaired by Mr. Milutinovic between Ambassador Hill, Professor Markovic, Professor Kutlesic, two members of the state delegation including the head of that delegation, calling for renewal and intensification of the negotiation process. That's from the testimony of Ambassador Petritsch at page 10800. You've already seen October 4th at the 6th Session of the Supreme Defence Council Mr. Milutinovic has called for what he hoped would be a reasonable resolution of the problem hoping that reason would prevail and there would be no air-strikes and if more needed to be done to fulfil the UN resolution then it should be done. There's also evidence from October, a meeting in Belgrade on the 24th and 25th of October in 1998, on which you've heard extensive testimony and there are numerous exhibits, primarily from General Naumann but also Sean Byrnes, a process that lasted over a two-day period. The relevant exhibits are P440, the 15 October 1998 Clark-Perisic air verification agreement; P432, 16th October, Geremek-Jovanovic OSCE-KVM agreement; P395, 25 October 1998 record of meeting; and P394 Byrnes-Djordjevic, KDOM-MUP understanding. P394 is the last one. Mr. Milutinovic was present at that time but what is the evidence about his role and what people remember about him? Well, General Naumann in P2561, his supplemental information, says this: "In the technical negotiations in October 1998, Mr. Milutinovic was present but not very active." Sean Byrnes, transcript 12155 to 12158, says that he recalls that there were 30 to 40 attendees at a plenary meeting. He says: "I recall the plenary was chaired by Mr. Milutinovic but my memory may be playing tricks on me." Now, at this point I will digress for a moment, Your Honours, and talk about the nature of the evidence in relation to the acts and conducts of Mr. Milutinovic. Mr. Naumann says Mr. Milutinovic was present and not active, and Sean Byrnes says his memory may be playing tricks on him in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. You'll also recall that Colonel Phillips testified in this court. He attended a meeting with William Walker and Slobodan Milosevic and he claimed that Mr. Milutinovic was present.
