He gave conflicting accounts of that meeting and he went from saying that he was pretty certain that Mr. Milutinovic was there to conceding that he may very well be wrong about that. Now, is there any -- is there evidence to suggest why Mr. Milutinovic may have been present at these meetings? The only evidence to that effect was given by Ambassador Vollebaek who was the head of the OSCE. He said he met three times with President Milosevic and that once or twice Mr. Milutinovic was present but he's vague and uncertain about that as well. In his testimony, P2634, he offers his understanding of why Mr. Milutinovic was present at some of these meetings, paragraph 39 he says: "I believe that this was to indicate that Kosovo was part of Serbia and that they did not want to talk about Kosovo without the president of Serbia present." Well, we know what's happening in the country at this time. There is armed insurrection there is an organised group that has taken up arms to achieve a political end, which is independence from Serbia and FRY. Surely the president of Serbia would be present, surely he would be informed, surely it was an internal matter. He would have to be there. We eel eve seen that he's already held himself out as a guarantor to the process. He's travelled to Kosovo on the 23rd of March. He's informed the government about results of meetings between Ambassador Holbrooke and Mr. Milosevic and he's been present. There's evidence he was present when General Naumann, General Clark, and Mr. Solana visited. We also saw that he received Ambassador Hill during the Hill process. We say that none of this evidence, none of this evidence, supports any allegation that the Prosecution alleges in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. He was the president of the republic after all, and his mere presence establishes nothing. Now, through the end of October and through November 1998, he's also present at meetings, the evidence tells us. He was at meetings where the security situation in Kosovo-Metohija is discussed and he's at meetings working to find a solution, a peaceful solution to the problems in Kosovo-Metohija. One exhibit is P2166 which purports to be the minutes of a meeting of the operations interdepartmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo-Metohija, 29 October 1998. There is a discussion on the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and the security situation generally. Mr. Milutinovic is present. And he is recorded as having made this intervention: "The president of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, considers that the reports submitted by the members of the Joint Command for Kosovo-Metohija should be accepted. He agreed with General Perisic's opinion that we are confront confronting two enemies today: Albanian secessionists and international community which is biased in their favour. He says we have done everything we were supposed to do to appease international factors, especially the US and NATO. The situation is as it is. We have accepted OSCE monitors but not foreign troops. We must not leave them to the Albanians. Our legal organs must ensure the necessary conditions for their unimpeded work. We must make them understand simply through the force of our arguments what the objective situation is so that they can depict it as such without any bias towards either side. "The OSCE mission consists of representatives of 53 states of Europe and the US and it is certain that not all of them are against us. President Milutinovic supported the proposal for consideration of the continued status of the Joint Command. Milutinovic believed that the Joint Command should continue functioning for a while, although that should be given -- although thought should be given to whether it should continue in its present membership or whether some changes should be made." That's at page 12 of those minutes. At page 14, "President Milosevic recommends that President Milutinovic, President of Serbia, go personally to Kosovo and explain the substance of the agreement which we have reached with the representatives of the international community to the presidents of the districts and municipalities. The president remarked that members of the OSCE monitoring mission cannot act arrogantly or seek wider authority than what has been agreed on." Well, on the 5th of November, 1998, President Milutinovic did travel to Pristina. The Witness Ljubinko Cvetic was present at that meeting that's 8187, 8189 of the transcript. He said Mr. Milutinovic attended the meeting. Other attendees included Mr. Stojiljkovic, the minister of the interior; Rade Markovic, the head of administration for state security. The witness said that Mr. Milutinovic reported that the Joint Command would remain in the same composition as when it was set up. Mr. Milutinovic played no other role at that meeting, according to the witness. And prior to the meeting Mr. Milutinovic met with political and business figures in Kosovo and Metohija. At the meeting Mr. Milutinovic explained the 11 points of the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement. He explained that the OSCE mission would include 53 countries, 2.000 monitors. Mr. Milutinovic spoke about the political and economic issues, saying that the Republic of Serbia would invest maximum efforts to help Kosovo, to help the situation in Kosovo, to be dealt with peacefully using political means. And before the break I'll deal with just one other segment of these submissions regarding the acts and conducts and we say the state of mind of Mr. Milutinovic in 1998. That has to do with the joint proposal for agreement on the political framework on self-governance in Kosovo and Metohija. 1D91, this joint proposal is dated 20 November 1998. Coupled with that is a declaration in support of this agreement, 1D18, page 372, which is 25 November 1998. This agreement and declaration is the culmination of a process that began in March 1998 with the establishment of the Markovic delegation. You recall I drew your attention to 1D204, the 11 points and timetable that were submitted to the UN Security Council, the 11 points and timetable that flow from the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement. Well, there that agreement -- the timetable said that by November the 2nd there would be the completion of an agreement containing the core elements for a political settlement in Kosovo and Metohija. Now, we know that during this time Mr. Milutinovic worked to support -- gave his continued support to this process in November. And I refer you to the 18th of November, 1D18, e-court pages 367, 369, it's a statement by Mr. Milutinovic in Pristina two days before the signing of the joint declaration. You have the full text of his statement; it's agreed to by the parties. He said that: "Serbia's committed to having the problems in KiM solved politically. Peace and common life are possible only with genuine, not formal equality of all national communities." He said that Serbia has reaffirmed both by state policy and at the diplomatic level that it's firmly committed to a political way of resolving the problems in Kosovo and Metohija. "Exactly for being consistent with this approach, I emphasise that Serbia is ready to fully defend and ultimately defend the achieved peace and safety of all its citizens." And regardless of the nonattendance of the Albanian representatives which was the case yet again, he said, "I stand personally ready to meet with them at any time and discuss the vital issues we discussed today." And of course the following day, on the 19th of November, in Belgrade, 1D89, Mr. Milutinovic met with minority leaders in Belgrade. Your Honour, I believe it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, we shall adjourn now and resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've been making submissions now for two hours, and we've worked out among ourselves that we would divide the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no need to be concerned about that at the moment, Mr. O'Sullivan. Just please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the break I was reviewing evidence that we say reflects the acts and conduct and state of mind of Mr. Milutinovic and I was taking you to 1998 and I move now to 1999. Paragraph 36(c) of the indictment says: "In accordance with instructions from Slobodan Milosevic, Milan Milutinovic was actively engaged in international relations." Well, first there's no evidence at all that Mr. Milutinovic was receiving instructions from Mr. Milosevic, and there's surely no evidence that he was taking instructions from Mr. Milosevic to engage actively in international relations. The Prosecution's position seems to be that at Rambouillet, the Serb delegation went there to obstruct and Mr. Milutinovic was there as a foil to ensure the breakdown of those talks to create I believe the Prosecution said "a window of opportunity" in their opening statement to commit crimes. Well, we've heard the evidence about Rambouillet. We know it to be quite different than what the Prosecution alleges. We've heard the evidence of Veton Surroi, a member of the Albanian delegation; we've heard the evidence of Wolfgang Petritsch, one of the three Contact Group negotiators; and there's a very large array of exhibits connected to Rambouillet through the testimony of both Mr. Surroi and Mr. Petritsch. The Court will recall that the relevant facts are that the Rambouillet-Paris talks were organised by the Contact Group, that the Serbian state delegation was sent to Rambouillet pursuant to conclusions of the National Assembly, that's 1D93, conclusions taken on the 4th of February, 1999, to send a delegation. P967 is a decision to appoint the delegation headed by the same Professor Markovic who had been heading the state delegation in 1998 and that a multi-ethnic delegation was sent to France consisting of Serbs, Albanians, Muslims, Turks, Goran, Egyptian, Roma. We know from the evidence that the conference in Rambouillet opened on the 6th of February. It was scheduled for one week with a possibility of extending it for a second week and ultimately it was extended for three more days after that. So between the 6th and the 23rd of February, 1999. The evidence is that Mr. Milutinovic was not a member of the delegation, but he arrived in Paris at the end of the first week, on the Thursday the 11th, according to Wolfgang Petritsch. At page 10848 of the transcript, Mr. Milutinovic was in Paris, he was housed in Paris. Ambassador Petritsch said he was informed that Mr. Milutinovic was an informal point of contact who occasionally dropped by the castle and was involved on a political level with the Contact Group foreign ministers. Mr. Petritsch acknowledged that Mr. Milutinovic basically had the same relationship to this delegation as he had to the Markovic delegation in 1998. We say he was a guarantor to the process. And what of the Serb state delegation? What we know from the -- from Exhibit 1D93, the conclusions of the National Assembly 4th of February, that it had a limited mandate. It [Realtime transcript read in error "He"] was empowered to negotiate a political framework of substantial autonomy and self-governance in Kosovo and Metohija. It had no authorisations to negotiate or accept implementation of a political agreement for the presence of foreign troops. I'm -- had it pointed out to me that the delegation was empowered by the National Assembly. Ambassador Petritsch testified that he was familiar with most members of the state delegation at Rambouillet because many of them had served on the 1998 state delegation. He said they were well-versed experts, aware of the minute details of the 1998 process and they worked constructively, and indeed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The uncertainty, Mr. O'Sullivan, is about your submission that he was, that's Mr. Milutinovic, was empowered to negotiate a political framework of substantial autonomy and self-governance; is that an accurate reflection of the submission you made?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, it's not and at line 13 I tried to correct that. It should be the delegation was empowered, not Mr. Milutinovic, the -- 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- 93 empowered the delegation. Mr. Milutinovic was not a member of that delegation. We know that on the 16th of February, that's the Tuesday of the second week, Serbian state delegation provided comprehensive and constructive comments to the political framework. And you will recall that only at this -- only the political framework was on the table during this period of negotiations. P563 is a diplomatic correspondence from Ambassador Petritsch to the foreign ministry in Austria. And also at transcript 10855 he said, "The Serbian delegation was ready to accept the political part of the agreement. It had been thoroughly negotiated and approved by the Contact Group." That's on the 19th of February. On the other hand, on the 18th of February, again, the Kosovo delegation, according to Veton Surroi, a member of that delegation, wanted to quit, had stopped working, because they disapproved of the latest draft of the Rambouillet Agreement that was handed to them by the negotiators on the 18th. 1D18, page 441-442, is a statement from the Kosovo delegation. And there their biggest complaint is that they were insisting on a binding referendum after three years and they complain that the preamble of the then-amended Rambouillet Agreement expressly included recognition of the sovereignty of the FRY. When we came to the 20th of February, that's the second Saturday which was supposed to be the last day of the two-week meeting, the foreign minister -- Contact Group foreign ministers met each delegation. Veton Surroi was in that meeting as part of the representatives of the Albanian delegation, before the Contact Group, and Mr. Thaqi, the head of that Albanian delegation, said that they rejected the political components of the Rambouillet Agreement and they could not accept the agreement without reference to a referendum, a referendum of independence after three years. That same day the Serb delegation came before the foreign ministers and that Serb delegation included Mr. Milutinovic. P2972 is the Milosevic transcript of Mr. Petritsch, and at page 10874 he says that Mr. Milutinovic told the first ministers of the Contact Group that the Serbs basically agreed with the political components. This led to a series of events which I wish to review with you which show quite precisely the true nature of the negotiations and the process at Rambouillet and certainly does not in any way lead to the conclusion or the inference that the Serb side was obstructive, or Mr. Milutinovic himself or anyone else there was obstructive in trying to find a peaceful and lasting solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, where is it we see that Mr. Milutinovic was a member of the delegation?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, he's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've twice now I think said he was or -- either that or was presenting the delegation's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, he was not -- he was not a member of the delegation, but on the 20th -- I misspoke earlier when I said "he." It should have been the delegation was empowered by the National Assembly that's what I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On the 20th, the Saturday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that, hold on a second. You said at 63, line 3, that he was a guarantor to the process and one of the Serb state delegates.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then what we know from Exhibit 1D93, the conclusions of the National Assembly that it had a limited mandate and it, rather than he, was empowered to negotiate a political framework but are you saying that he was part of the delegation?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, he was not part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- of the delegation. He was -- he came the end of that first week to Paris and Ambassador Petritsch told us that he had -- that he was an informal point of contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's his role when he goes before the Contact Group to explain the Serb position?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The Contact Group had summoned both sides together to see whether or not they accepted the political framework they had negotiated up to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but what was his status in presenting the Serb position?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He, along with two or three other members of that Serb delegation, came before the foreign ministers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, following that meeting on the 20th of February where the Serbian delegation had expressed their general agreement with the political framework and the Albanian side had rejected it, Veton Surroi told us that there were deep divisions within the Albanian delegation that went from having Mr. Thaqi opposing the agreement and working to stop it to having other members by the 22nd or 23rd of February also opposed to the political components of the agreement. This led to a meeting between Madeleine Albright and members of the Albanian delegation on the 21st of February, including Mr. Surroi, at which meeting Mr. Surroi suggested that perhaps Madeleine Albright could provide a side letter to the Albanian delegation, offering the US interpretation of the words "will of the people" which is in the final clause of the Rambouillet Agreement. The request was to have Mrs. Albright confirm that the term "will of the people" would be tested in a referendum three years after the termination of the Rambouillet Agreement, a referendum to be conducted by the people of Kosovo. That's 1D18, page 449. Mr. Surroi and Mr. Petritsch confirmed that Mr. Surroi approached Wolfgang Petritsch seeking a similar side letter from the EU. Mr. Petritsch learned, as did Mr. Surroi, that the EU would not approve such a letter, Russia was opposed to it, and certainly the FRY would be. The evidence is that that letter was withdrawn, the draft letter prepared by Mrs. Albright addressed to the Albanian delegation, which brought us to the last day of the meetings in Rambouillet, the 23rd of February. And there there's a series of events which we say exposes exactly what was happening there. On the morning of the 23rd of February, at 9.00 a.m., the negotiators presented both delegations with what they call the final version of the Rambouillet Agreement which included for the first time chapters 2, 5, and 7 on implementation. Court exhibit IC126 is a table of the Rambouillet agreements and it shows that these -- this table corroborates the evidence showing that implementation chapters 2, 5, and 7 are tabled for the first time to the parties on the morning of the 23rd of February. And the cover letter asks for a response by 1.00 p.m. that day. 1D98 is the -- a full copy of that agreement with a cover letter signed by the three Contact Group negotiators: Ambassador Petritsch, Hill, and Mayorski and the letter indicates that the Russian Federation had not approved chapters 2 and chapter 7 of the implementation portion of this newly tabled agreement, and Mr. Mayorski, Ambassador Mayorski makes that express in his signature under which he says that he does not, or the Russian Federation does not adopt 2 and 7. There was still problems, however, by -- for getting support from the Albanian side to agree to the agreement, the political side of the agreement, that leads to 1D18, page 467, which is a letter from the Albanian delegation to Madeleine Albright. It's a mirror image of the letter that was rejected and vetoed by the EU, Russia and would not be accepted by the FRY. We know the circumstances surrounding that. Veton Surroi was in the room, the delegation room, the Albanian room, where it was taking place. Ambassador Hill and his assistant Jim O'Brien and other representatives were preventing Hashim Thaqi from seeing the interpreter's computer on which the letter was being drafted. The letter was signed by Veton Surroi. Now, the letter is published in a book we have in evidence, 1D18, by Professor Weller who was an advisor to the Albanian delegation. And yet, when professor -- when Ambassador Petritsch testified, he was much less than candid or truthful about this letter, in fact initially denied that he knew about it. And then later he admits that he knows it. Now the transcript page 10889 he says it was a transparent process, all documents are tabled, there were no documents, agreements, side deals, side letters that were not tabled. He only knew about the first Albright letter which was withdrawn, he knows of no side agreements or side deals. Ambassador Petritsch was being untruthful, Your Honours, because when he was confronted with the letter from the Albanian delegation by Mrs. Albright signed by Veton Surroi 1D18, page 467, he conceded that he knew about the letter, that he knew about it after the meetings were concluded. At the same time, on the same day, the 23rd of February, 1D18, 466, there's a letter from the Serb delegation to the negotiators of the Contact Group at 1600 hours, that's document number 34 in 1D18, page 466. Ambassador Petritsch describes that as a constructive letter. The delegation says it's prepared to discuss the scope and character of international presence and that all elements of self government at the time of the finding of the agreement have to be known and clearly defined. The evidence further from Ambassador Petritsch is that there were three letters submitted by the Serb delegation to the Contact Group negotiators. And I refer you to the first letter which is 1D18, page 466, it's document 31. And at the transcript 10932 that letter was reviewed with Ambassador Petritsch and he says that he understood the position of the Serb delegation, that there was general agreement to the political framework, the areas requiring future negotiation on the political framework were identified, that points needed refining. He acknowledged that it was a legitimate position for a federal state to take in relation to the political components and that more time was needed to discuss implementation. And yet the common perception and the allegation by the Prosecution is that the Serb side is to blame for the failure at Rambouillet. We know from Mr. Surroi and Mr. Petritsch that Madeleine Albright had threatened that if the Albanian side sign and the Serbs don't, then Serbia will be bombed. We know there's Russian disapproval for chapters 2 and 7, tabled at the 11th hour. We know that there's a side deal between Mrs. Albright and the Albanians, contrary to what has been told publicly or within the confines of that negotiating complex. The Serb letter is constructive, willing to continue to discuss the scope and character of international presence and to refine the political agreement. The public declarations are that the Albanians have accepted the deal and the Serbs have rejected it. Now, we also know from witnesses like John Crosland, the British attache in the FRY, that throughout 1998 there was open support for the KLA, that there was support for a regime change in Belgrade, and that the Rambouillet process proceeded on that basis. Now taken alone Mr. Crosland's evidence may not mean that much but when seen in the light of all the events, one can see exactly the way things proceeded and that the Serb delegation is certainly not to blame for any failure at Rambouillet. And Mr. Milutinovic denounced that process. He, as well as others, denounced the process, but denouncing this process in no way can be said to be an example of any criminal intent or any criminal conduct. He was just calling the situation as he saw it. There's one other aspect, important aspect, arising out of the evidence at Rambouillet through the evidence of Wolfgang Petritsch. Mr. Petritsch claims that he was at a meeting with Mr. Milutinovic and Ambassador Mayorski, and at this meeting Mr. Petritsch claims that Mr. Milutinovic said that if Serbia's bombed there will be massacres in Kosovo. Mr. Petritsch understood that to mean there would be massacres of Albanian citizens -- Albanian civilians by Serbs. In our submission, this is evidence which is incapable of belief and not entitled to any credence under the law of Rule 98 bis. To get right to the point, when asked by the Presiding Judge, His Honour Lord Bonomy, whether he recalled Mr. Milutinovic actually saying these words or whether he was rationalising it based on a diplomatic correspondence, Ambassador Petritsch says he was rationalising it. He says this must have been said because it was recorded in a diplomatic dispatch. That dispatch is in evidence, it's P562, Austrian diplomatic correspondence. Now, Ambassador Petritsch saw this diplomatic correspondence for the first time just prior to his testimony in this trial. On two occasions at page 10883 he said it was drafted by his assistant Jan Kickert, and that Jan Kickert was present during an OTP interview conducted with Ambassador Petritsch in May 1999. We know that this correspondence was reflecting the situation as at 6.00 a.m. on the 20th of February, 1999. It was prepared overnight between the 19th and 20th of February, 1999. We know that this correspondence passed through two sets of hands and it was an encrypted e-mail sent from Paris to Belgrade to Vienna. Well, what do we know? Let's put this in context, shall we? The OTP interview conducted in May and June 1999 is P2792. Ambassador Petritsch claims he used his best efforts to give a detailed and accurate account of events as he remembered them. He does not mention Mr. Milutinovic saying if bombs fall there will be massacres in Serbia or in Kosovo. He attributes that to a man named Stambuk. He claims he was taken aback by this statement of Mr. Stambuk and it left a distinct impression on him. When Ambassador Petritsch testified in the Milosevic case, transcript Exhibit P2793, nothing is said about Mr. Milutinovic in relation to bombing leading to massacres. He attributes this once again, Mr. Petritsch does, to Mr. Stambuk. If you look at the account of his testimony in Milosevic and his account attributing this phrase to Mr. Milutinovic, they're virtually identical. The context and the circumstances is virtually identical. They're discussing, according to Mr. Petritsch, the necessity of implementation, demilitarisation of the KLA, negotiations ending, and then the comment about bombing leading to massacres. Jan Kickert testified in this trial as well. Now, we've seen that Ambassador Petritsch claims that Mr. Kickert wrote P562. Mr. Kickert claims that Ambassador Petritsch must have added the paragraph or the annotation regarding Mr. Milutinovic's alleged comment about bombing and massacres. Of course Mr. Petritsch never offered such an explanation when he testified. He was given every opportunity to say that he himself added this passage and he didn't. With Mr. Kickert, the circumstances surrounding the preparation of P562 were reviewed, that's from pages 11253 to 11256. The Chamber will see that it was a very hectic day, all through the day and all through the night, and then at 6.00 in the morning, final touches were put on this document and sent off. So they worked all night -- all day and all night after midnight to prepare this document and Mr. Petritsch says that he rationalises that Mr. Milutinovic must have said it because he has no recollection of it and he bases that entirely on having seen this exhibit for the first time just prior to his testimony here despite the fact of being interviewed by the OTP months after Rambouillet, having testified in Milosevic where he never attributes these words to Mr. Milutinovic. We say that this evidence is not worthy of belief. Now, I've been covering the acts and conduct and state of mind chronologically of Mr. Milutinovic and we've covered the point up to the Rambouillet-Paris process in March 1999. I now turn to the final period, the one beginning on the 23rd of March, 1999. I wish to review that evidence with you. I've already made submissions in relation to the Supreme Defence Council and the Supreme Command. We've seen that on the 23rd of March, P1738 are the amended rules of the Supreme Defence Council, where there's an expanded quorum and decisions are made by consensus. We also know that there's no evidence in this case that the Supreme Defence Council met after the 23rd of March, 1999. And it's our submission that there's no evidence in this case that Mr. Milutinovic was a member of a body known as the Supreme Command. There is evidence, however, regarding a session of the National Assembly of Serbia on March 23rd, 1999. At that Assembly, Mr. Milutinovic, among others, addressed the Assembly. We have in evidence and will review that, the conclusions and the minutes of the National Assembly. We also have the evidence of Ratomir Tanic in connection with this event. Before turning to the National Assembly, I wish to say a few words about Tanic, who we say also under Rule 98 bis jurisprudence is incapable of -- his testimony is incapable of belief and it could not properly sustain a conviction; it's not worthy of your belief. Let me highlight a couple of examples. Mr. Tanic claims that he only testifies when the information he provides to the Court is corroborated by two or three independent sources. 1D27 is the Milosevic transcript, page 5025; 1D28 is the Milosevic transcript, 5105-5106 and 5092; and he said this in our trial at page 6497. Mr. Tanic was reprimanded by this Trial Chamber for refusing to answer a question at 6460-6461. Tanic was evasive and dishonest about the most basic things: His educational background, his criminal record, his personal record as a member of a political party where he claims he was an important member. But what does he say about the National Assembly meeting on the 23rd of March? He claims two things. He claims that Mr. Milutinovic, during his address to the National Assembly, tried to delude the Yugoslav public by saying that NATO wanted to intervene in Yugoslavia under its own flag. And the second thing he says is that draft conclusions of the Assembly prepared by Mr. Vuk Draskovic, the deputy prime minister of the FRY at the time, which had previously been agreed to by Mr. Milutinovic according to Tanic, that these conclusions were modified in order to mislead the public and the National Assembly. Well, in evidence we have 1D32, which are the minutes of the National Assembly and include the conclusions. They're agreed by stipulation between the parties. I asked the Chamber to look at this document, and you'll see that Tanic's claims are incorrect and incredulous and not worthy of belief. First, Mr. Milutinovic's speech. He spoke 12th out of 24 individuals that day. The main speaker was Ratko Markovic, the head of the state delegation, who provided a report of the state delegation on the talks in Rambouillet and Paris. And if you read his intervention, you'll see that the report made by Mr. Markovic is entirely consistent with the evidence in this case. Mr. Milutinovic spoke at page 2931 of Exhibit 1D32. This is an oral submission and I won't read it -- read the extract to you. It's short. I ask you to do so. But what does Mr. Milutinovic refer to? Well, he refers to the implementation chapters, 2, 5, and 7, of Rambouillet; he refers to the insistence of a referendum after three years by the Albanian side; and the insistence of foreign troops, the NATO troops -- the insistence of foreign troops, NATO troops, in a sovereign country. Now, we know the Rambouillet agreement contemplated NATO troops. It was not agreed to at Rambouillet by the Russian Federation and certainly there was no UN mandate for foreign troops in Yugoslavia. And what are the conclusions? Well, 1D32, the minutes, from pages 56 to 58, set out the conclusions of the Assembly that day. The so-called Draskovic proposal led by -- through Tanic has, in fact, three exhibit numbers. I'll give you all three P710, P2482, P2483. I invite the Chamber to review these conclusions, both the ones in the minutes and the ones that are drafted by Mr. Draskovic. They're virtually identical. And in fact, the conclusions contained in the minutes of the Serbian Assembly are more far-reaching and conciliatory. And one more point about the minutes in 1D32, page 12, a man named Spasoje Krunic, a member of the Serbian Renewal Party, that's Mr. Draskovic's [Realtime transcript read in error "^"] party. He's on the commission which drafted the conclusions which were actually adopted that day by the Serbian Assembly. So there's nothing misleading, malevolent, or criminal about what happened in the Assembly that day. There was an Assembly session. At page 76, line 10, Mr. Krunic was a member of the Serbian Renewal Party, that's Vuk Draskovic's party. And Mr. Krunic was a member of the committee that drafted the conclusions adopted that day. So there's nothing misleading about what occurred in the Assembly that day, not Mr. Milutinovic's speech, not the Assembly conclusions. Mr. Tanic has it wrong. Mr. Tanic also said in -- during his testimony that Mr. Milutinovic supported the idea of going to war, that's page 6324 of the transcript. There's a bold assertion by Tanic that Milutinovic supported the idea of going to war. There's nothing in his testimony or there's no evidence aside this bald assertion in evidence to support that. In fact, everything that we've reviewed today, Your Honour, points the other way, that Mr. Milutinovic did what he could to avoid a war, to find a peaceful solution, and to encourage others to do the same. Tanic also testified that Mr. Milutinovic, in 1998, distorted information going abroad. That's pages 6336, 6337. That somehow Mr. Milutinovic was preventing peace. This is another fanciful assertion by Mr. Tanic unsupported by any evidence. As we've seen, all the evidence shows a completely different view. Mr. Milutinovic never spread any distorted or any incorrect information abroad. Tanic also said that Mr. Milutinovic was part of a private chain of command at 6372. I think we can do away with that bit of evidence by the comment made the Presiding Judge who found the account to be nothing more than something a journalist could have written and deserves the same value from the Bench as any piece of journalism. Mr. Tanic also gave evidence about a cease-fire. 1D36 is the joint statement of the FRY and Serbia on a cease-fire; it's agreed by way of stipulation. Mr. Tanic gives four versions of these events, which I'll describe in a second, and what we say is an incredulous explanation as to why there are four different versions of the events. The cease-fire, according to Mr. Tanic, was supposed to be implemented on Catholic Easter, which was one week before Orthodox Easter. Indeed, the -- the evidence is that the cease-fire was implemented between the two Easters. Well, what's relevant here, we say, is the way in which Mr. Tanic testified and the way he tries to implicate people in things. This is the first version of his account which is P2480, his statement, paragraph 125. There Mr. Tanic says he called Mr. Milutinovic personally to discuss the cease-fire. In a second version, in his supplemental information, Tanic says he called Mr. Milutinovic and told Mr. Milutinovic that Dusan Mihajlovic wanted to speak to him. Then there's a third version in 1D27, the Milosevic transcript, page 6465, there he said, Mr. Tanic says he overheard Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Mihajlovic on a speaker-phone. And the fourth version that he gave in court is that Mr. Mihajlovic was using a special phone to call Mr. Milutinovic in a secret command post. And how does he explain the inconsistencies, the different versions? He says, well, at page 6466, he says, "The gist is the same but it's true that it's a bit confused because I do not have very precise recollection. Well, it took us quite a while to find him. It was wartime, you know, and this is why confusion created. I corrected that in my talks with the Prosecution and the gist was the same that Milutinovic -- that we had not finished the job. The gist of the conversation is the same. Of course, it is depicted in a confused manner as to the circumstances. I do have this kind of problem because many events happened and some of them bear emotionally on me. In my statement, the gist has never changed. Circumstances are described differently; this is of course due to my memory which works under the burden of hundreds of events stored in there." This is an incredulous fabrication. He back-pedals constantly when he tries to explain things. He spends his whole time trying to hoodwink people, Your Honour. There's also evidence during the war given by Mr. Merovci and also a 92 quater statement from Dr. -- the late Dr. Rugova. There are two exhibits I wish to point out here, one is P416, that's a joint statement signed by Mr. Milutinovic and Dr. Rugova in April 1999; and 1D60 is a video -- is video footage of the statements given by Mr. Milutinovic and the late Dr. Rugova, after that statement was signed. Well, the whole context of this is that the authorities had arranged for the safe transfer of Dr. Rugova, Mr. Merovci, and their families to Rome during the war. They left the country in May 1999. Mr. Merovci testified that his family was allowed to travel to Macedonia in early April after meeting with Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade, phone lines were reconnected in Pristina, they were allowed to phone abroad, they did so. Dr. Rugova met with ambassadors, he met with clerics. And the upshot is that the life of an important Albanian leader was saved and his family was. He was released, allowed to travel abroad, out of harm's way. The joint statement for P416 calls for an end to the NATO bombing and resumption of negotiations, seeking a peaceful resolution and a political agreement on Kosovo and Metohija. There can be no suggestion or inference that Mr. Milutinovic was engaging in any kind of criminal conduct or criminal intent in this regard. Recently, the Prosecution has entered into evidence four documents which I think bear some comment. They are P2842, P2844, P2843, and P2828. These are letters. The first three deal with vital statistics and the preparations for a census. P2842 is a two-page letter from Vladan Kutlesic, the deputy prime minister of the FRY to the director of the Republic Bureau of Statistics dated 6 October, 1998. A copy was sent to Mr. Milutinovic's office. P24 -- 2844 is a letter from the Republican Bureau of Statistics of the Republic of Serbia, dated 17 February 1999. And 2843 is a report dated 12 January, stating that there's no conclusive reliable information available about the ethnic population -- the ethnic Albanian population in Kosovo and Metohija since the 1961 census. Now, Your Honour, when you read through these -- this correspondence, you'll also see that a census was planned between the 1st and 15th of April, 1999, to get accurate numbers. Well, that was pre-empted by the war. And when -- one fails to see how any of this is even relevant to any sort of criminal intent or criminal conduct that when a census is being organised to meet international standards, as these documents suggest, and that in fact a census throughout Serbia, including Kosovo, is being planned for the month of April 1999, one is left pondering. The fourth letter is P2828, and it's a two-page letter sent by the president of the provincial board of the SPS in Kosovo and Metohija, the copy sent to the Office of the President of the Republic of Serbia, on the 19th of June, 1998. It deals with the murder of a 68-year-old Serbian man and with terrorists bringing weapons into Albania -- weapons from Albania. The letter states that the Serbs are slowly losing faith in their state and its organs and they're scared. At best, this is a letter from a local politician who's expressing his concerns about dealing with terrorism. There is no logical inference or any connection to be made between this letter and any allegations or any charges, any wrong-doing, by Mr. Milutinovic. I move to one other area, to two pieces of legislation. 1D136 is a law on rescinding of the laws by which the temporary measures for social protection of the self-management rights and socially owned property were imposed. Now, this law from 1991, Article 1, amends the law enacted in 1989 on temporary measures for protection of self-management rights and protection of socially owned property. We've made submissions in this case that the laws enacted during the time of the SFRY are irrelevant to this case because that state ceased to exist. Firm, this 1D136 amends that law, abolishes that law. The law was to -- cease to exist by 31 December 1991. Now, for the sake of completeness you also have to refer to 1D138, and 1D138 extends the time for the abolishment of the 1989 provisions, it extends it to 31 December 1992. So by the end of 1992, the 1999 [sic] provisions are abolished. By the end of 1992, the 1989 provisions are abolished. And lastly, 1D37 is the law on cessation of work of the public legal office of self-management which, again, the public legal officers ceased to function under the 1989 law. Now, I hasten to add that the Chamber knows that during this period in the early 1990s Mr. Milutinovic was the SFRY ambassador to Greece. He had no political affiliations, no evidence of any political affiliation, and he's a high-ranking civil servant, public servant, ambassador to Greece at this time. I turn now to my concluding comments, submissions. Mr. Milutinovic under 7(1) is charged with ordering. The actus reus of ordering is: "The accused as a person in a position of authority instructed another person to commit an offence." There is no evidence to this and no inference can be drawn from the evidence in this case in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. He's charged with planning under 7(1). The actus reus of planning is: "The accused alone -- the accused alone or together with others designed the criminal conduct constituting the crimes charged. The planning was a factor substantially contributing to the perpetration of the crimes." We say there's no evidence to support that allegation and no inference from the evidence can be drawn in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. He's also charged with instigating. The actus reus of instigating is: "The accused prompted another person to commit the offence. The instigation was a factor substantially contributing to the conduct of the other persons committing the crime." No evidence, no inference can be drawn from the evidence in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. The mens rea for these three offences is quite similar that: "The accused acted with direct intent or with the awareness of the substantial likelihood that a crime would be committed." No evidence pointing at all to Mr. Milutinovic in this regard for any of the underlying alleged offences. Mr. Milutinovic is charged with aiding and abetting. The actus reus of aiding and abetting is: "The accused gave practical assistance, encouragement, or moral support which had a substantial effect on the perpetration of the crime." The mens rea is that: "The accused knew his acts would assist the commission of the crime by the perpetrator or he was aware of the substantial likelihood that his acts would assist the commission of the crime by the perpetrator." There's no evidence and no inference can be drawn from the evidence in relation to the acts, conduct, and state of mind of Mr. Milutinovic. He's charged with committing as a co-perpetrator in a JCE. Categories 1 and 3 under our jurisprudence. The law states that there must be -- that there are three base requirements for a conviction of JCE. First, a plurality of persons is required; second, the existence of a common purpose, which amounts to or involves the commission of a crime provided for in the statute; and third, the participation of the accused in the common purpose is required. There's no evidence of a common purpose, we say. There's no evidence of Mr. Milutinovic being in a plurality of persons who as part of a common purpose. They alleged that the common purpose is the expulsion -- the permanent expulsion of the Albanian population from Kosovo and Metohija. There's no evidence to support that. The mens rea of the first category, the basic joint criminal enterprise, "it must be shown that the accused or other participants in the JCE intended that the crime at issue be committed." The Prosecution can point to no evidence suggesting that on the part of Mr. Milutinovic. The mens rea of the third category of the extended category of JCE speaks of alleged crimes outside the common purpose, the extended foreseeability of it. We say there's no evidence in this case that the Prosecution can point to in relation to this second or third category of JCE. And what of superior authority under Article 7(3)? There's no evidence of any superior-subordinate relationship, de jure or de facto, between Mr. Milutinovic and any of the alleged perpetrators of base crimes. There's no knowledge, there's no evidence that he had knowledge or had reason to know that crimes were about to be committed or that they had been committed, and as for acquiescence, there's no evidence that Mr. Milutinovic had any means at his disposal, even if he were a superior, to prevent or punish. I started these submissions by saying under 98 bis a motion will succeed if there's no evidence supporting a particular count, or if the only relevant evidence is so incapable of belief that it could not properly sustain a conviction, even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution. Your Honour, there's no evidence of criminal conduct or criminal intent, no exercise of de jure or de facto power or influence, no exercise of authority or any connection to the alleged base crimes. Mr. Milutinovic asks you to acquit him of all five counts. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I support what has been said by my esteemed colleague, Mr. O'Sullivan, as regards the facts and law. The Defence of Nikola Sainovic will attempt to show why it considers that the Prosecutor has failed to prove his case against Nikola Sainovic and why -- I do apologise. There is a part in the factual submissions I will not agree with in what Mr. O'Sullivan has said. So I agree with what he has said pertaining to the law rather than the facts. The Defence of Nikola Sainovic will attempt to draw attention to those parts of the indictment against Nikola Sainovic which it feels have not been proved even if it were accepted without any doubts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The indictment against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the interpreter is asking you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Slow down. It is -- this is a difficult one to judge, but I think you're going to have to speak more slowly than you would normally do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The indictment against Mr. Sainovic contains a large number of allegations concerning his alleged role in the events of 1998 and 1999. The Prosecution has tried to prove some of these allegations, but with reference to a considerable number of allegations the Prosecution has failed to offer a single piece of evidence, a single word in the testimony of a witness, or a document which would at least indirectly confirm what is stated in the indictment about Sainovic's role. In the indictment, it is stated that Sainovic was the representative of Slobodan Milosevic for Kosovo. Not a single witness has confirmed this, nor has said anything about this. Of course, there are no documents to prove this. The only thing we have heard so far, as mentioned by Mr. O'Sullivan, is that he was the -- the fact that the second vice-president or vice-premier of the principal government is mentioned as Milosevic's advisor for Kosovo. That he was a Special Envoy for Kosovo, that is. It is further stated in the indictment that throughout the time-period relevant for the indictment there was a Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija and at the head of this command was Nikola Sainovic. More than a hundred witnesses have testified here and not a single one mentioned that in 1999 Nikola Sainovic was at the head of the Joint Command for Kosovo. Also, moreover, several thousand documents have been admitted into evidence, but not in a single one of these does it say that at the time relevant for the indictment Nikola Sainovic was at the head of the Joint Command. The indictment covers events starting on the 1st of January, 1999, and, as has been said, in this time-period there is no evidence to show that Sainovic was at the head of anything that might be called a Joint Command. Let me emphasise that there is also no evidence to show that Sainovic was a member of an organ that allegedly existed and waged the operations in Kosovo and Metohija, which might be called Joint Command. So he was neither its president nor commander nor member; nobody ever said anything like this. What has been shown by the evidence adduced, as observed by Your Honours, is that the circumstances, structures, state organs, officials, their powers and activities differed substantially in 1998, as compared to 1999. In 1999 there was a NATO intervention and an imminent threat of war was declared in the state, followed by a state of war. These two facts imply a fundamental difference as regards the role and responsibilities of the state organs in their joint efforts to defend the country from the NATO air-strikes. Many witnesses, especially - and I insist on this - witnesses who are members of international organisations and bodies active in Kosovo in 1998, have described Mr. Sainovic's role. They have mostly done this by talking about their impressions which were often formed based an hearsay, newspaper reports, or solely on the fact that Mr. Sainovic often spoke to them or negotiated with them. Sainovic was often the only person they had contacts with. He was also - and we do not deny this - a high-ranking official in the federal government, one of the five vice-presidents, and therefore, the highest highest-ranking person in the FRY with whom they had contacts. That is why some of them arrived at the erroneous conclusion about the importance of Sainovic's role in Kosovo. They did this without having any insight into the way in which the policy of Serbia and Yugoslavia was formulated, the way processes of information took place between the competent organs, what the mutual relationships between these organs were, what the formal and what the de facto competences were on particular protagonists on the Serbian and Yugoslav political scene. These foreigners saw Sainovic and thought that he was an important person; however, they had no way of knowing how important he really was and they didn't know this. What I'm saying about foreign representatives refers only to the year 1998. As regards 1999, especially the period of the 24th of March, 1999, these witnesses were not in Kosovo. They weren't physically there, so they had no knowledge and they were not able to have any knowledge about events in Kosovo. Therefore, they could not know anything about any role Mr. Sainovic might have had. Even if there was some form of coordination between the VJ, the Army of Yugoslavia, and the MUP in the course of 1999, I maintain that this coordination did not include any civilians, politicians, or state officials who would be able to command VJ or MUP units or their joint operations. Therefore, in 1999 Nikola Sainovic did not have any role which might be in any way linked to coordination of the Army of Yugoslavia. Moreover, all the witnesses who testified before this Chamber spoke about the intact chains of command, both in the army units and among the members of the MUP, both in 1998 and in 1999. I am not listing their names because there was not a single one who spoke to the contrary. Whether there was any kind of Joint Command in the context of some of the documents admitted into evidence which refer to 1999, whether or not there was anything like this, one must bear in mind that these are documents which were in fact documents issued by the VJ, the Army of Yugoslavia. This is evident from their content and the fact that these documents refer solely and exclusively to the use of army units. There is not a single document dating from 1999 drawn up in the MUP bearing the letterhead of some kind of Joint Command. There is no such document dated 1998 either, and it's not there because it doesn't, in fact, exist. Also, there is not a single document emanating from a civilian body which might be said to be any kind of briefing or report or anything like that emanating from a Joint Command. Also, in no document is there any mention of any kind of civilians interfering or attempting to influence the intact chains of command we have mentioned, nor is there any trace of this in military or police reports relating to the relevant time-period. It is also important to mention that there is not a single report, letter, or briefing before you of any commander belonging to any kind of Joint Command in 1999. There is no headquarters, no commander of any such Joint Command. The chain of command was intact. It is very important to bear in mind that Nikola Sainovic was the deputy prime minister of the federal government, which did, in fact, have certain powers over the Army of Yugoslavia, both in 1998 and 1999. But no competencies whatsoever in relation to the MUP of Serbia or the MUP of Montenegro because the police was fully under the jurisdiction of each of the republics. In Exhibit P1468, which was admitted into evidence after six months of justified, in my view, refusal and which refers to the period from July to October 1998, which, let me point out, is before Mr. Sainovic was appointed president of the federal commission for cooperation with the OSCE, there is not a single note or entry in that document ending with an order. If this was the Joint Command, we never see the words "the command orders the following." There is no reference to a previous order, as would be normal. If one day you issue an order, the next day you want to follow-up and see what happened. If there was a command, it would have to issue orders, it would have to have a commander, a log-book, a headquarters. And there would be at least one document emanating from that command dated 1999, bearing the letterhead of that Joint Command. But there is no such document because no such document ever existed. On the contrary, from these notes mentioned in Exhibit P1468, one can see that there was an exchange of information in order to get a better overview of the situation. There is something that is not sufficiently clear. I said that in 1998 there was not a single document with the same content as the 14 or 15 documents dated 1999, saying "I order that ..." As I said, there were meetings that were held for the purposes of exchanging information in order to gain a better overview of the situation. One might refer to this as coordination, as was done by Mr. Sainovic in his interview which I refer you to. That is coordination between politics, the army, and the police. In 1998 there was no state of war. The federal government had no powers over the work of the police, either in Serbia or in Montenegro. Take a look at the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council. Some have been quoted here. You will see that there are no members of the police present. Why? Because the federal state had no competences over the police. They would have had to be the interior ministers of Serbia and Montenegro, but they are not there. And the generals of the police but they're not there. The Government of Yugoslavia had only a logistical role but not a command role. In the time-period in which a state of war was declared, the Government of the FRY had no role in command and control as relates to the defence forces, and therefore its vice-president had neither actual nor formal duties in relation to military operations. In a state of war, it is the president of the FRY and the military structures with their intact chain of command who have these powers. The Prosecutor said that Nikola Sainovic was the representative of Slobodan Milosevic for Kosovo because diplomats and representatives of the international community were often told to go and talk to Sainovic about Kosovo. It's true that many of them did, but it's also true that they did this because the federal government established a commission for cooperation with the OSCE mission, and Sainovic was appointed president of that commission by that government. Before this, Sainovic was the deputy prime minister in the federal government with special duties in international relations; first of all, the implementation of Dayton and then Kosovo. There is no evidence, nor has anybody ever said, nor was it possible for anyone to say that Sainovic was some kind of personal representative of Milosevic, as if we were talking about a company, a commercial enterprise, or a terrorist organisation. Sainovic was doing this because it was his job, and he was one of five vice-presidents, as was Zoran Lilic who did not come to testify here. And many witnesses have confirmed this. I'm tired of repeating all their names. It is not correct to say that Sainovic had an active role in negotiations on forming the OSCE mission, or more precisely, that his role differed from the roles of dozens of other officials who were doing that job and had similar roles. Many of them were mentioned, Stambuk and others. Something else is true, however, and that is that Sainovic in the implementation of that agreement tried to do everything in his power to have the agreement complied with, to replace the conflict with political negotiations with a mediation of the international community in order to achieve peace in a multi-ethnic Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor says that Sainovic acted as a liaison between Milosevic and the leader of the Kosovo Albanians. What is correct, however, is that Sainovic did nothing but convey messages. Let us recall the testimony of Adnan Merovci. When asked by this Defence about his understanding of the role of the accused, whether Sainovic was a middleman who simply transmitted messages or whether he was a decision-maker, Witness Merovci replied that in his view Sainovic was a person, I quote, "who was acting as a middleman who simply conveyed the positions of high-ranking officials." This was stated on the 17th of January, 2007, on page 8535, lines 18 to 19. Nikola Sainovic is charged with participating directly or indirectly in a joint criminal enterprise, with the aim of changing the ethnic balance in Kosovo. But I wonder, Your Honours, what the contribution was of Nikola Sainovic to the aims of this alleged joint criminal enterprise. In order for an enterprise to exist there has to be a plan, and the plan has to be implemented. In these ten months I have heard nothing, and neither have you, that might indicate that such a plan actually existed, that such a goal existed; and least of all, even if something like that did exist, that Sainovic was part of it. We have also not heard that if there was no explicit plan, there was something that might be referred to as a plan, the existence of which might be inferred from all the circumstances of this case. Something, for example, like a tacit agreement or deal amounting to an agreement. If there was a plan, let us now surmise that, in any form whatsoever that I just referred to, the question is: What act did Nikola Sainovic commit in this period of -- starting with the 24th of March, 1999, that would contribute to the implementation of this joint plan if any such plan did, in fact, exist. What have we heard from the witnesses? What have we read in the documents that the Prosecution has presented to us about such acts -- any such acts or activities by Sainovic in the period after the 24th of March, 1999, that would affect the events or would in any other way contribute to the implementation of this hypothetical criminal plan or design, whether within the framework of this design or going even beyond such a framework. Let us assume for a moment that somebody says something in a meeting and this might be interpreted as the instigation to a prohibited activity. Does that mean, according to the Prosecution or the Judges, that any persons present at the meeting are to be held responsible as members of the JCE even if they had not heard those remarks? The Prosecution -- the Defence considers that responsibility has to contain the personal attitude, personal view, acts or omissions, and that everything else is mere interpretation that goes way beyond the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and international humanitarian law in general. This Tribunal must not put aside the obligation of the Prosecution to prove the kind and the degree of individual responsibility, and in the case of Nikola Sainovic the Prosecution has failed to do that. This Tribunal must not allow for the lower limit of the joint criminal enterprise to be set at a level that would equate individual responsibility with collective guilt. Because it is contrary to the elementary moral and philosophical norms that modern criminal law is based on. The Prosecution has failed to prove the existence of any vertical chain of command, a relationship of subordination and superiority between Sainovic on one hand and the VJ and MUP on the other in the period relevant for the indictment, and even indeed in the period that precedes the indictment, 1998 in other words. When we talk about the joint criminal enterprise, we have to answer the question whether there was intent to commit a crime. The Defence contends that the Prosecution has failed to prove that Sainovic had the intent to commit any criminal offence, war crime in this case, and indeed that there was an intent that Sainovic shared with the other participants of the joint criminal enterprise for the acts alleged in the indictment. It is particularly interesting that the Prosecutor claims that the joint criminal enterprise came into being in October 1998 at the latest and that it continued -- that its existence continued throughout this period relevant for the indictment. This is the period that goes beyond the so-called Joint Command minutes for 1998, this is, as my colleague Mr. O'Sullivan quoted, when it was actually specified or stated that hostilities had ceased and so on and that the Joint Command should continue in existence. This is the period in which various agreements are reached, Holbrooke-Milosevic, Geremek-Jovanovic, Clark-Perisic and so on. This is the time when Sainovic becomes the chairman of the Federal Commission for Cooperation with the OSCE. Is this the joint criminal enterprise? Is this when it started? To say that about Mr. Sainovic is absurd. Your Honours will remember that a number of witnesses gave evidence to the fact that Sainovic did everything to find a peaceful and political solution for the crisis, particularly at the time when the Prosecutor alleges that there was this joint criminal enterprise and when this criminal plan was in the making. Witness Michael Phillips says, and I quote: "Sainovic was sincere about trying to find a strategy for the co-existence for the Serbian and Albanian population to live together." This is 19 March 2007, page -- at page 11887, lines 9 through 11. Witness Byrnes explicitly stated before this Chamber that Sainovic had told him all he could in the negotiations, in the ongoing negotiations. At the time he gave striking testimony about Nikola Sainovic's real intentions. He said, and I quote: "I believed in that," his intentions, "I believed everything he told me." 16th of April, 2007, at page 12191, lines 17 through 18. Furthermore, when the Defence asked whether Sainovic considered that the situation in Kosovo should have been solved by political means, Witness Byrnes said that it was his clear impression from the conversations with the accused that, I quote: "He, as a practical politician, tried to find a mutually acceptable political solution for the problem and that he was working in that direction." 16th of April, 2007, at page 12188, lines 15 through 19. When the Defence asked Ambassador Petritsch whether he agreed with the conclusion that a high degree of consensus had been achieved between him and Mr. Sainovic in relation to efforts to solve the crisis, in other words, that it should be achieved through political and peaceful means, he said yes and he said that he, Sainovic, hoped that it would be possible -- I quote: "That it would be possible to achieve an agreement by peaceful means on the basis of the Kosovo Verification Mission and instruments that were in existence at the time." That's 2nd of March, 2007, at page 10947, lines 19 through 23. How is it possible that somebody who sincerely is trying to contribute to find a peaceful solution for the crisis, as those witnesses indicate, at the same time shares the goals of a joint criminal enterprise that should be implemented through a widespread and systematic campaign of terror and violence, deportations, murder, forcible transfer of the population, and persecution. Well, isn't it clear that Sainovic was the man who trying until the very last moment at Rambouillet to take even the smallest chance for a negotiated solution for the conflict. Sainovic tried to negotiate even with the KLA representatives. In his evidence, Witness Byrnes noted that Sainovic launched this initiative - and I quote - "to extend a hand to the KLA leadership in an effort to find some kind of a solution." And that Sainovic saw such a meeting as something that could be used as a basis for - and I quote - "broader political consequences." That's 16th of April, 2007, at 12189, lines 1 through 16. Sainovic is trying to do all he can to find a solution at Rambouillet to prevent the worst from happening. As I've already noted, Witness Byrnes explicitly said that he had believed in what Sainovic had said, that Sainovic had been doing all he could to prevent further escalation of the conflict in Kosovo. That's on 16th of April, 2007, at 12191, lines 15 through 18. Before this Chamber, Witness Petritsch commended Sainovic for his cooperative attitude, saying that meetings with Sainovic were always - and I quote - "amicable meetings based on mutual respect." Witness Petritsch stressed in particular that he met with Sainovic at Rambouillet frequently and that Sainovic was - I quote - "of use" to him and that he had the impression that -- that he had the impression that - I quote - "Sainovic listened and tried to provide answers to the demands made by the international community and he concluded that those meetings were conducted in a very pleasant atmosphere and that this is something that sticks in his memory, 2nd of March, 2007, at 10945, lines 14 through 24. Generally speaking, Ambassador Petritsch stressed in his evidence that Sainovic was a man of peace, I quote, and that somebody else prevented the peaceful solution for which -- which both Sainovic and head of the delegation Ratko Markovic advocated. Those other factors that Sainovic had no control over, according to Ambassador Petritsch, made it impossible to achieve an agreement, and Ambassador Petritsch gave evidence about the last night of the negotiations in Rambouillet and further developments in Paris where Sainovic kept silent, as he said. And I say again that when Ambassador Petritsch went to the last round of negotiations with Milosevic, Sainovic was not there because he fell out of grace because of his views. And now we have this other person appearing, Milosevic's Special Envoy. So who can say then that Sainovic shares the objective to change the ethnic balance in Kosovo by violent means and at the same time advocating the general exchange of prisoners? In his evidence, Ambassador Petritsch stresses that Sainovic worked -- made efforts in goodwill to free the -- to achieve the release of KLA prisoners, saying that he was sure, and I quote, "Mr. Sainovic proposed to Mr. Milosevic to make a positive decision in this issue." And in his view this was a constructive move on the part of Mr. Sainovic. 2nd March, 2007, at 10946, lines 20 through 23. Again, when the Defence asked Witness Byrnes whether he agreed that Sainovic saw the release of the prisoners as an opportunity to calm the situation and to pave the way to a real peaceful solution, Witness Byrnes agreed with this suggestion, adding that Sainovic saw this in such a way that he considered that an exchange of prisoners could perhaps lead to something greater; 16th of April, 2007, at page 12189, lines 17 through 22. Generally speaking, the Defence would like to ask the Trial Chamber to look in detail at the evidence provided by those three witnesses in their entirety as they relate to Mr. Sainovic. Such high-ranking persons such as Ambassador Petritsch and people of that rank could not say things that are not accurate. Sainovic also advocated the return of the population to their homes with the increase of the international presence as we could see in the example of Malisevo. In his evidence before this Trial Chamber, Witness Phillips underlined or stressed that Mr. Sainovic was of great assistance in the efforts to solve the Malisevo problem, 19th March, 2007, at page 11877, lines 2 and 3. The Defence would also like to refer to evidence by Jan Kickert, providing some kind of supplemental clarification for the evidence provided by Ambassador Petritsch, who also described what Nikola Sainovic was doing. Let me remind you that according to the Prosecution, this witness was supposed to prove Sainovic's criminal role by dint of helping to provide electricity in the building where the representatives of the international community were -- had their premises, when they failed to pay their electricity bills. That's 7th of March, 2007, page 11190, and then further 11191, but we will, I hope, forgive him for this crime. In this context, it is of special interest to note whether the accused really knew whether a criminal offence alleged in the indictment was committed. This was to be a natural and foreseeable consequence of a JCE. From the context of the evidence presented, particularly the evidence that relates to an overview of criminal offences committed on the ground, it is quite clear that the local commanders failed to report all the -- any crimes even to their immediate superiors. How could then Nikola Sainovic know about such crimes and how could he be expected to know that the possible outcome of his acts would be criminal? For instance, General Vasiljevic in his testimony states that he visited the security organs of the Yugoslav Army in Kosovo and that he concluded at the security administration of the Yugoslav Army that there were no omissions in the work of the military police, that there were no omissions in the work of the military police and the security organs in the Pristina Corps, and that they were, in fact, to be commended for their results. 24th of January, 2007, at page 8977, line 4, to page 8978, line 5. So if the organs that were duty-bound to detect the perpetrators of criminal offences worked very well, as Vasiljevic testified, and if their superior officers had no objections to their work and they did not have such objections, how could Sainovic be expected to know or to have to know about any crimes whose perpetrators had not been -- had not been covered in any reports or had not been criminally prosecuted for their crimes? As far as the police is concerned, at meetings that Sainovic participated in, if you look at the minutes you will see that in any debate he, in fact, advocated efforts to prevent crimes and if any crimes were committed that the perpetrator should be punished. And this is the most that he as a politician could do. Let me repeat that the federal government had no jurisdiction over the police because this was something that was in the jurisdiction of the republic. Let me remind you of Exhibit P1996, this is the minutes of the MUP headquarters dated 7th of May, 1999, and P1989, the minutes of the MUP headquarters dated 4th of April, 1998. This is what I'm talking about. The Trial Chamber has to determine -- oh, I have to apologise. It's 1999, the 4th of April, 1999. The Trial Chamber has to establish the basic elements of the criminal intent of the accused in the context of the joint criminal enterprise. What can the Trial Chamber establish regarding Sainovic's intent except to accept what witnesses Byrnes, Phillips, and Petritsch say in the response to the questions the Defence asked them in order to establish Sainovic's true intent. In a nutshell, it was Sainovic's intent to have negotiations replace conflict and that a peaceful multi-ethnic Kosovo should be achieved through political agreement. In the indictment in paragraph 24 the Prosecution alleges that Sainovic commanded the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia via various organs, including the Joint Command with him at its head. This is an arbitrary claim by the Prosecutor who composed this indictment and it fails to meet the fundamental criteria for the evaluation of evidence at this stage of the proceedings, as no proof whatsoever has been adduced to support it. The standard we are referring to is the standard in Rule 98 bis. That Sainovic commanded the forces of Serbia and Yugoslavia in 1999 was never mentioned by anyone, nor can it be found written down anywhere, nor can such a conclusion be made from anything before us. In paragraphs 46(a) and (b) and in paragraph 47(b) of the indictment, it says that Sainovic, as the deputy prime minister of the Government of the FRY in charge of Kosovo, implemented the powers given to him by Slobodan Milosevic over the Army of Yugoslavia with regard to Kosovo, including authority over the VJ and the MUP and civilian bodies. Quite simply, nobody ever said anything like this, nor did anyone ever write anything like this, nor was anything like this possible because one must bear in mind that the FRY was a well-organised state with its organs and institutions. The Defence now asks the Chamber to put aside these issues to save me the trouble of trying to prove how absurd this is. In paragraphs 46(c), (f), and (i), and in paragraph 47(a) of the indictment, it says that Sainovic was the head of the Joint Command and that through that command he commanded control, directed, and otherwise exercised effective control over forces of the FRY and Serbia. Let me repeat. In 1999 there are no indicia that Sainovic had any such role. Most of the Prosecution case relating to Sainovic's role is an attempt to use analogy in an impermissible manner in order to equate 1998 and 1999. Some evidence which has been erroneously interpreted and which refers to 1998 and the role of certain civilian persons who were sent to Kosovo has been used in an attempt to show that there was a uniform manner of acting in the time-period before the indictment and the time-period to which the indictment refers, and analogy is impermissible in legal proceedings. Whatever existed in 1998 in the period from July to October need not have existed, necessarily, in 1999. Quite simply, a Joint Command never existed, either in 1998 or in 1999 with Nikola Sainovic as its commander or member. With reference to 1999, there is mention of documents bearing the letterhead "Joint Command," but they do not show that there are any civilians connected with that. And this includes Sainovic. Even General Vasiljevic stated in his testimony that Sainovic attended a meeting and that somebody else told him that this was a meeting of the Joint Command. But when referring to Sainovic's role at that meeting he says that he simply does not know what it was. When asked by the Defence whether he allows for the possibility that, at the meeting in Pristina, Sainovic represented the federal government, Vasiljevic answered that he did not exclude such a possibility and he said, I quote, "You will reach your own conclusions about this." He didn't say who he was addressing. And this was the 22nd of January, 2007, page 8837, line 2. The Defence wishes to draw attention to the fact that part of Vasiljevic's notebook hasn't been admitted into evidence although in his interview to the OTP Vasiljevic explicitly said he did not take any notes at that meeting. In that meeting it says that this was actually a meeting in the command of the Pristina Corps. So the words "Joint Command" do not appear in the notebook either. With relation to paragraphs 46(d) and (e) of the indictment, in the evidence adduced there is no mention of the fact that at the time the indictment refers to, Sainovic participated in any kind of planning, coordination, or ordering of operations or planning, instigating, or ordering the concealment of crimes. In paragraph 46(g), Sainovic is linked up with volunteers. The federal government and its vice -- deputy prime minister have no competences concerning volunteers, nor has any kind of role played by Sainovic been shown in connection with volunteers. Of special interest is paragraph 46(h), as well as paragraphs 47(f), (g), (h), (i), and (m), where it is claimed that Sainovic instigated and legitimised crimes perpetrated against Kosovo Albanians by failing to report and investigate crimes or by failing to punish or discipline members of the forces of the FRY and Serbia. Nowhere is it explained what kind of competencies Sainovic had to conduct investigations, what competencies did Sainovic have to punish anyone? This is pure speculation in the indictment and it remains speculation after we have heard all the evidence that the Prosecutor has decided to present in his case, because we have not heard a single word in this courtroom about Sainovic being able or allowed to carry out any kind of investigation, especially to punish anyone or discipline anyone. He had no such powers, and this is best seen in his discussions which have already been mentioned, where he recommends the prevention of crimes and the punishment of perpetrators. He said this as a politician, as a deputy prime minister of the federal government, and that was the most he was able to do. And this is actually what he did. I have finished one part. It seems to be time for a break, but let me mention on page 98 to 2 [as interpreted], 97 line 24, the name of Bugarcic is missing, this is the person who replaced Sainovic at the negotiations. I will have 20 minutes, not more.
